lessons.title: P0 to P3: build the day one phase at a time
lessons.summary: Split the grow-day into four phases, learn what starts and ends each one, and tell forecast shots from shots that really ran.
outcomes: Put P0 wait, P1 refill, P2 maintain and P3 overnight in order on a grow-day.
Explain what ends P0, what P1 aims for and what triggers a P2 or rescue shot.
Tell a forecast of shots from the event record of shots that ran.

slides.title: Four phases across the grow-day
body: One grow-day runs from lights-on to the next lights-on
Four phases: P0 wait, P1 refill, P2 maintain, P3 night
slides.narration: Think of a working day: arrive, warm up, keep going, then go home. A grow room has a daily rhythm too, set by its lights. Lights-on is the time the grow lights switch on. Lights-off is the time they switch off. One grow-day runs from one lights-on to the next lights-on. For example, with lights on at six in the morning, the grow-day lasts twenty-four hours, until six the next morning. The app splits each grow-day into four parts called phases. A phase is one stage of the day with its own job and its own rules. Look at the strip. The four phases are labelled P zero, P one, P two and P three: wait, refill, maintain, then dry back overnight. Knowing the order lets you read any day on the graph. Next, the first phase.

visual.title: Four phases across the grow-day
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: Lights-on is 07:00 and lights-off is 19:00. When does this grow-day end?

options.text: 07:00 the next morning
options.feedback: A grow-day runs from one lights-on to the next lights-on.

options.text: 19:00 the same day
options.feedback: Lights-off ends the lit hours. The grow-day runs on to the next lights-on.

options.text: Midnight
options.feedback: The app follows the lights, not the calendar date.

slides.title: Wait first: P0 morning dryback
body: At lights-on each zone starts P0: no water
P0 ends at its dryback target or its maximum wait
slides.narration: At lights-on, every zone starts in P zero, the morning wait. No water is given, so the root zone keeps drying, like a sponge draining before you top it up. Lesson A four called this fall dryback. P zero aims for a dryback target. A target is the value a phase is trying to reach. P zero ends at the first of three events. The dryback reaches its target. Or the VWC falls to the P two re-water threshold, which you meet on slide four. Or the time limit runs out; the app calls that limit the maximum wait. For example, lights-on is six in the morning, the maximum wait is ninety minutes, and drying is slow. Six o'clock plus ninety minutes is half past seven, so P zero ends by then at the latest. That is why lights-on alone cannot tell you when the first shot comes.

visual.title: Wait first: P0 morning dryback
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: Lights-on is 06:00 and the maximum wait is 120 minutes. Drying is slow. What is the latest P0 can end?

options.feedback: 120 minutes is two hours. 06:00 plus two hours is 08:00.
P0 starts at lights-on. It waits for its dryback target or its time limit.
120 minutes is two hours, not one hour and twenty minutes.

slides.title: Refill: P1 ramp-up
body: P1 refill: shots with pauses between them
Each shot lifts VWC a step toward the P1 target
slides.narration: The second phase is P one, the refill. The app calls it ramp-up. The Controller gives a series of shots, one watering each, with a pause between them. Each shot lifts the VWC a step, like filling a bath one bucket at a time. The refill aims for the P one target. For example, P zero ended at fifty-four percent and the target is sixty. That is six percentage points to climb. If each shot lifts the reading about two points, six divided by two gives about three shots. Some water drains, and the probe sees only part of the pot, so the real count can differ. To know how many shots ran, read the record of shots, not the drawing. Next, the long middle of the day.

visual.title: Refill: P1 ramp-up
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: P1 starts at 50% VWC, the P1 target is 59%, and each shot adds about 3 points. Roughly how many shots?

options.text: About 3
options.feedback: 59 minus 50 is 9 points. 9 divided by 3 is about 3 shots.

options.text: About 9
options.feedback: 9 is the gap in points. Divide it by 3 points per shot.

options.text: About 20
options.feedback: Find the gap first: 59 minus 50 is 9 points, then divide by 3.

slides.title: Maintain: P2 and the re-water threshold
body: P2: a shot each time VWC falls to the re-water threshold
Shots drawn on a planning chart are a forecast
slides.narration: The third phase is P two, maintain. Think of cruise control: the car holds its speed instead of speeding up. P two holds the VWC near the top of the refill. It uses a threshold called the re-water threshold. Each time the VWC falls to that line, the Controller can give one shot. Some screens label it the re-water point; it is the same line. For example, the refill ends at sixty percent and the re-water threshold is fifty-seven. That is a three-point fall. If the zone dries two points an hour, three divided by two gives one and a half hours between shots. The planning chart draws shots at that spacing. A drawing of shots the plan expects is called a forecast. If the zone dries more slowly, fewer shots happen, and that is normal.

visual.title: Maintain: P2 and the re-water threshold
labels: A shot each time it is hit
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: P2 refills to 62%, the re-water threshold is 58%, and VWC falls 2 points an hour. Forecast gap between shots?

options.text: 2 hours
options.feedback: 62 minus 58 is 4 points. 4 divided by 2 points an hour is 2 hours.

options.text: 4 hours
options.feedback: 4 is the fall in points. Divide by the rate of 2 points an hour.

options.text: 8 hours
options.feedback: Divide the 4-point fall by the 2-point hourly rate, do not multiply.

slides.title: Worked example: a 06:00–18:00 lighting day
body: 06:00 lights-on: P0 starts the grow-day
P0 → P1 → P2 hand-overs depend on readings
18:00 lights-off: every zone moves to P3
slides.narration: Now put the phases on a clock. Our example room has lights on at six in the morning and lights off at six in the evening. Six in the morning plus twelve hours is six in the evening, so the lights are on for twelve hours. At six in the morning, each zone enters P zero and waits. When P zero ends, P one refills, then P two maintains. Those hand-overs depend on the readings, so the clock cannot give their times. At lights-off, six in the evening, every zone moves to P three, whatever phase it was in. The Controller can also start P three a little earlier, so the night's dryback finishes by morning. P three lasts until six the next morning, twelve hours later, when a new grow-day starts. Expect phases by their order, not by fixed clock times.

slides.title: Overnight: P3 and the Rescue floor
body: P3: overnight dryback, normally no water
Below the Rescue floor, a rescue shot can run
slides.narration: The fourth phase is P three, the overnight dryback. The lights are off, and normally no water is given. The root zone dries slowly, like a sponge left on the sink overnight. One protection stays awake. In lesson B one you dragged a night-time emergency threshold. Growers call that line the emergency floor. In the app it is labelled Rescue floor, and this course uses that name from here on. If the VWC falls below the Rescue floor overnight, the Controller can give a rescue shot. A rescue shot is a small protective shot that stops the root zone drying too far. For example, with the floor at thirty-five percent, a reading of thirty-six gets no shot. A reading of thirty-four is below the floor, so a rescue shot can follow. Treat the floor as an alarm line, never as a level to aim for each night.

options.text: A rescue shot, because the zone is in P3
options.feedback: Being in P3 gives no water by itself. The floor triggers the rescue.

options.text: A rescue shot every hour by default
options.feedback: Rescue shots follow the floor, not the clock.

body: Wait = P0, refill = P1, maintain = P2, night = P3
Forecast = planned shots; event record = real shots
slides.narration: Pause and fill the gaps. The morning wait is P zero, and the maintain phase is P two. Now picture a room lit from eight in the morning. Eight in the morning plus twelve hours is eight in the evening, so lights-off is at eight in the evening. P zero starts at eight in the morning. P three runs from eight in the evening to eight the next morning. The P one and P two times stay unknown until the readings decide them. Last, separate two lists of shots. A forecast shows the shots the plan expects. The event record lists the shots that really ran, with their times. When you check what happened, read the event record. The next lesson shows how a slider tilts these settings toward one kind of growth.

options.text: Ten

lessons.title: Vegetative and generative: a bias, not a magic switch
lessons.summary: Use a dimmer picture to learn vegetative and generative steering, then calculate how the slider blends two endpoints in a profile.
outcomes: Explain vegetative growth, generative growth and steering bias, separate from growth stage.
Calculate a slider blend between two endpoint values and round it to the step.
Check a profile's sharing and EC fields before trusting a slider change.

slides.title: Think of a dimmer
body: Vegetative growth: roots, stems and leaves
Generative growth: flowers and fruit
Steering bias: the direction you intend
slides.narration: Think of a dimmer switch. It does more than switch a light on or off. It slides smoothly between the two. Keep that picture for this lesson. A plant puts its effort into two broad kinds of growth. Vegetative growth builds roots, stems and leaves. Generative growth builds flowers and fruit. Growers can nudge that balance through watering. A planned nudge toward one side is called a steering bias. Bias is your intention, separate from the plant's age. A young plant and a flowering plant can each get either bias. For example, a grower may give a flowering plant a vegetative bias for a week to help it grow more leaf. The plant decides how it responds, so you watch the crop as well as the settings. Next: how watering does the nudging.

visual.title: Think of a dimmer
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: A plant is flowering. Can it be given a vegetative bias?

options.text: Yes; bias is your intent, separate from growth stage
options.feedback: Stage is what the plant is doing. Bias is the direction you choose.

options.text: No; flowering plants must use generative bias
options.feedback: Stage does not lock the bias. Growers choose it for a purpose.

options.text: Only when VWC is above 60%
options.feedback: Bias is not set by one reading. It is a planned direction.

slides.title: How watering nudges the plant
body: Smaller drybacks tend toward vegetative
Larger drybacks tend toward generative
Light, climate, substrate and variety also matter
slides.narration: How does watering nudge the plant? Think of the sponge again. Smaller drybacks keep the root zone more evenly wet. In suitable conditions, that tends to support vegetative growth. Larger drybacks let it dry further between shots, which tends to support generative growth. For example, compare a zone drying from sixty to fifty-seven percent each morning with one drying from sixty to fifty-one. The first fall is three points, a gentler, more vegetative pattern. The second is nine points, a more generative pattern. EC, light and climate also push the balance. So do the substrate, the plant variety and its growth stage. These are tendencies, so check the crop as well as the numbers. Next: how the app stores a set of numbers for each direction.

visual.title: How watering nudges the plant
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: Zone A dries from 60% to 58% each morning. Zone B dries from 60% to 50%. Which leans more generative?

options.text: Zone B, with the 10-point dryback
options.feedback: Larger drybacks tend toward generative growth.

options.text: Zone A, with the 2-point dryback
options.feedback: Smaller drybacks keep it wetter, which tends toward vegetative.

options.text: Neither; dryback has no effect
options.feedback: Dryback size is one of the main ways watering nudges the balance.

slides.title: Endpoints, profiles and the slider
body: Endpoint: a full set of settings for one end
Profile: both endpoints saved together
Slider: 0 = vegetative, 100 = generative
slides.narration: Now the dimmer becomes a setting in the app. Picture two complete sets of numbers, one for each end of the range. Each set is called an endpoint. The vegetative endpoint holds the settings you want for a fully vegetative day. The generative endpoint holds the settings for a fully generative day. Together, the two endpoints are saved as a profile, so you can reuse them. Between them sits the slider, a control you drag from zero to one hundred. Look at the scale. Zero uses the vegetative endpoint. One hundred uses the generative endpoint. Fifty sits halfway, so each setting lands halfway between its two endpoint values. The app calls this mixing a blend. You choose the endpoint values yourself, because the app cannot work them out from your pot size. Next, a blend worked step by step.

visual.title: Endpoints, profiles and the slider
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: Maximum wait endpoints: 30 min vegetative, 50 min generative. The slider is at 0. What wait does the app use?

options.text: 30 minutes
options.feedback: Right. 0 is the vegetative end, so the app uses that endpoint as it is.

options.text: 40 minutes
options.feedback: 40 is the halfway blend, at slider 50. At 0 the app uses one end only.

options.text: 50 minutes
options.feedback: 50 is the generative endpoint, used at slider 100, the other end.

slides.title: Worked example: halfway
body: Endpoints 30 and 50 min; slider 50
Then round to the setting's step
slides.narration: Work one setting through. Take the maximum wait from lesson B two, the longest P zero can last. Say the vegetative endpoint is thirty minutes and the generative endpoint is fifty. First, find the difference: fifty minus thirty is twenty minutes. Next, turn the slider into a fraction: fifty out of one hundred is one half. Then take that fraction of the difference: half of twenty is ten. Last, add it to the vegetative endpoint: thirty plus ten is forty minutes. The app then rounds the result to the setting's step, the smallest change that setting accepts. With a one-minute step, forty stays forty. A result of forty point four would round to forty. The same four steps work for every setting in the profile. Next, you try one.

visual.title: Worked example: halfway
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Blend fictional maximum-wait endpoints of 30 and 50 minutes at slider 50.
steps: Difference: 50 − 30 = 20 minutes.
Fraction: 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5.
Blend: 30 + 0.5 × 20 = 40 minutes, then round to the step: 40.
workedExample.answer: 40 minutes. Whether 30 and 50 suit your crop is a separate choice you make.

check.prompt: Endpoints are 10 and 30 minutes, the slider is 50 and the step is 1 minute. What is the blend?

options.text: 20 minutes
options.feedback: Difference 20, half of it is 10, and 10 + 10 = 20.

options.text: 10 minutes
options.feedback: 10 is half the difference. Add it to the first endpoint, 10.

options.text: 40 minutes
options.feedback: Do not add the endpoints. Take half the difference and add it to 10.

slides.title: Your turn, with the steps supplied
body: Equal endpoints give the same value everywhere
slides.narration: Your turn, with the steps laid out. Keep the endpoints at thirty and fifty minutes, and set the slider to twenty-five. Pause and work it out before you listen on. The difference is still twenty minutes. Twenty-five out of one hundred is one quarter. One quarter of twenty is five. Thirty plus five is thirty-five minutes. Now a special case. Suppose both endpoints are thirty minutes. The difference is zero, and any fraction of zero is zero. So the setting stays at thirty wherever the slider sits. Existing set-ups often start this way, because both endpoints copy your current settings. If the slider seems to change nothing, check whether the endpoints are equal.

visual.title: Your turn, with the steps supplied
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: Both endpoints are 45 minutes. You move the slider from 20 to 80. What happens to the setting?

options.text: It stays at 45 minutes
options.feedback: Equal endpoints have zero difference, so every position gives 45.

options.text: It rises to 80 minutes
options.feedback: The slider is a position, not minutes. With equal endpoints nothing moves.

options.text: It doubles to 90 minutes
options.feedback: The blend moves between the endpoints and never beyond them.

slides.title: Try a new pair on your own
body: The slider is a position, not minutes
slides.narration: Now try one on your own. The endpoints are twenty and sixty minutes, and the slider is at seventy-five. Work it out first, then check. The difference is sixty minus twenty, which is forty minutes. Seventy-five out of one hundred is three quarters. Three quarters of forty is thirty. Twenty plus thirty is fifty minutes. Notice the trap: seventy-five is a position on the slider, not a time. It never goes into the answer as minutes. The blend tells you the setting the app will use. Whether that setting suits your plants is a separate question, which you answer by watching the crop.

visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: Endpoints are 40 and 80 minutes and the slider is 75. What is the blend?

options.text: 70 minutes
options.feedback: Difference 40; three quarters is 30; 40 + 30 = 70.

options.text: 75 minutes
options.feedback: 75 is the slider position, not a time.

options.text: 30 minutes
options.feedback: 30 is the increase. Add it to the first endpoint, 40.

slides.title: Check the profile before you trust it
body: A shared profile changes every zone that uses it
Check which EC each field means
A slider change is a draft until saved and switched on
slides.narration: Last, three checks before you trust a slider change. First, a profile can be shared. Several zones or weeks can use the same profile. Edit it once, and every one of them changes. So before you edit, look at which zones use it. Second, check each EC value in the profile. Lesson A five showed that feed EC and pore-water EC are different measurements, so confirm which one each field means. Third, moving the slider makes a draft, like the draft threshold in lesson B one. The plan on screen updates at once. Nothing changes in the grow room until the plan is saved and switched on, steps a later lesson covers. Now explain the dimmer aloud, then try the practice. The next lesson works out how much water each shot delivers.

visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: Zones 1 and 2 share a profile. You raise its generative maximum wait from 50 to 60 minutes. Whose plan changes?

options.text: Both zones’ plans
options.feedback: A shared profile feeds every zone that uses it. Check users before editing.

options.text: Only the zone you had selected
options.feedback: The edit is to the profile, and both zones read from it.

options.text: Neither; profiles cannot be edited
options.feedback: You can edit endpoint values. That is why sharing matters.

lessons.title: How much water did each plant get?
lessons.summary: Treat drippers as small taps, calculate water per plant and per zone from flow and runtime, then separate delivery from runoff and uptake.
outcomes: Read L/h as litres per hour for each dripper.
Calculate water per plant and per zone from the effective runtime.
Explain why delivered water is not runoff, uptake or a promised VWC rise.

slides.title: A dripper is a small tap
body: A dripper lets water out slowly at the plant
Flow rate in litres per hour: L/h
2 drippers × 4 L/h = 8 L/h per plant
slides.narration: Picture a garden tap left running. The water that comes out in a set time is its flow rate. In a grow room, each plant is fed by drippers. A dripper is a small nozzle on a thin pipe that lets water out slowly at the plant. Its flow rate is given in litres per hour, written L slash h. Four litres per hour means four litres would come out in one full hour. Look at the picture. Each example plant has two drippers, each rated at four litres per hour. The zone has twelve plants. So each plant gets two times four, which is eight litres per hour. The printed rating is a starting figure. A catch test measures the real flow: you collect one dripper's water in a cup for a timed period and measure it. Next, flow becomes a shot volume.

visual.title: A dripper is a small tap
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: A plant has three drippers rated 2 L/h each. What is its flow rate?

options.text: 6 L/h
options.feedback: 3 drippers × 2 L/h = 6 L/h for the plant.

options.text: 2 L/h
options.feedback: That is one dripper. Multiply by the 3 drippers.

options.text: 5 L/h
options.feedback: Multiply the number of drippers by the rating: 3 × 2 = 6.

slides.title: Worked example: thirty seconds
body: Runtime: how long a shot runs
1 hour = 3600 seconds
slides.narration: A shot runs for a set time, called its runtime. Our example shot has a runtime of thirty seconds. The flow rate is per hour, so first count the seconds in an hour. Sixty seconds times sixty minutes is three thousand six hundred seconds. Each plant gets eight litres per hour. Multiply eight by thirty to get two hundred and forty. Divide by three thousand six hundred. The answer is about zero point zero six six seven litres. Multiply by one thousand to get millilitres: about sixty-six point seven millilitres per plant. That is less than a small glass of water. Keep the unrounded figure for the next step, so later answers stay accurate.

visual.title: Worked example: thirty seconds
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Estimate one 30-second shot with two 4 L/h drippers for each of 12 plants.
steps: Per-plant flow: 2 × 4 = 8 L/h.
Per-plant water: 8 × 30 ÷ 3600 = 1/15 L ≈ 66.7 mL.
Zone water: 1/15 × 12 = 0.8 L.
workedExample.answer: About 66.7 mL per plant and 0.8 L per zone, if every dripper gives its stated flow.

check.prompt: A plant gets 6 L/h and the runtime is 60 seconds. How much water does that plant get?

options.text: 0.1 L, which is 100 mL

options.feedback: You multiplied but did not divide by 3600 seconds per hour.

options.text: 6 L
options.feedback: 6 L would take a full hour. 60 seconds is one sixtieth of that.

slides.title: Scale from one plant to twelve
body: Per zone = per plant × number of plants
1/15 L × 12 = 0.8 L per zone
Double the runtime, double the water
slides.narration: So far you have worked out one plant. The zone has twelve plants, all fed the same way. Multiply the per-plant amount by twelve. Use the exact fraction, one fifteenth of a litre, rather than the rounded figure. One fifteenth times twelve is zero point eight litres for the whole zone. Per plant tells you what one pot received. Per zone tells you what the whole group used, which matters for the tank. Now double the runtime to sixty seconds. At the same flow, the water doubles too: zero point eight times two is one point six litres per zone. To total a whole day, add up only the shots in the event record, the shots that really ran.

visual.title: Scale from one plant to twelve
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: One shot gives 0.05 L per plant. The zone has 20 plants. What is the zone total?

options.text: 1 L
options.feedback: 0.05 × 20 = 1 L for the zone.
That is one plant. Multiply by the 20 plants.
20 is the plant count, not litres. Multiply it by 0.05.

slides.title: A shot's share of the pot
body: 45 s × 8 L/h ÷ 3600 = 0.1 L per plant
0.1 L ÷ 5 L × 100 = 2% of substrate volume
The probe may rise by less than 2 points
slides.narration: How big is a shot compared with the pot? Take a separate example: a forty-five-second shot on the same two drippers. Eight times forty-five is three hundred and sixty. Divided by three thousand six hundred, that is zero point one litres, or one hundred millilitres per plant. Each pot holds five litres of substrate. Zero point one divided by five is zero point zero two. Times one hundred is two percent of the substrate volume. You might expect the VWC to rise two points. Often it rises less, or unevenly, because some water drains out and the probe samples only one spot. Use two percent as a size guide, and read the probe to see the real response.

visual.title: A shot's share of the pot
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: A shot gives 0.3 L to a pot holding 6 L of substrate. What share of the substrate volume is that?

options.feedback: 0.05 is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for percent.
Divide the shot by the pot volume; do not multiply them.

slides.title: Your turn: complete the calculation
body: 1 × 3 L/h × 60 s ÷ 3600 = 0.05 L per plant
0.05 L × 12 = 0.6 L per zone
Note it: rated flow or catch test?
slides.narration: Your turn. Each plant has one dripper rated at three litres per hour, and the shot runs for sixty seconds. The zone has twelve plants. Pause and work it out before you listen on. One dripper at three litres per hour gives three litres per hour per plant. Three times sixty is one hundred and eighty. Divide by three thousand six hundred: zero point zero five litres, or fifty millilitres per plant. Times twelve plants is zero point six litres per zone. Last, note where the three litres per hour came from. Was it the printed rating, or a catch test? Write that beside the answer, so the next reader knows how firm the number is.

visual.title: Your turn: complete the calculation
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: Two drippers at 1.5 L/h each run for 120 seconds. How much water per plant?

options.feedback: That uses one dripper. The plant has two, so 3 L/h.
Check the flow: 2 × 1.5 is 3 L/h, not 6.

slides.title: Use the time that actually ran
body: Requested runtime: the time asked for
Effective runtime: the time that actually ran
Always calculate with the effective runtime
slides.narration: Sometimes a shot does not run as long as asked. The Controller has a safety limit on how long one shot may last. The time asked for is the requested runtime. The time that actually ran is the effective runtime. For example, a shot requests one hundred and twenty seconds, but the limit is sixty seconds. The effective runtime is sixty. Each plant gets eight litres per hour. Eight times sixty, divided by three thousand six hundred, is about zero point one three three litres. That is about one hundred and thirty-three millilitres. Using the requested time would give about two hundred and sixty-seven millilitres, double the real figure. So always calculate with the effective runtime. The app shows both times side by side.

visual.title: Use the time that actually ran
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: A shot requested 90 s, but the limit cut it to 45 s. Flow is 8 L/h per plant. Which estimate is right?

options.text: 0.1 L, using 45 s
options.feedback: 8 × 45 ÷ 3600 = 0.1 L. Use the time that actually ran.

options.text: 0.2 L, using 90 s
options.feedback: 90 s was requested but never ran. That doubles the real figure.

options.text: 0.15 L, the average of both
options.feedback: Do not average. Only the effective 45 s delivered water.

slides.title: Recall: delivery, runoff, uptake
body: 2 × 3 L/h × 90 s ÷ 3600 = 0.15 L per plant
0.15 L × 15 = 2.25 L per zone
Delivery is not runoff, and not uptake
slides.narration: Last, three words that sound alike but mean different things. Delivery is the water the drippers supplied. Runoff, from lesson A five, is water that drains out of the pot. Uptake is water that enters the plant. A flow-times-runtime calculation gives delivery only. Try one more. Two drippers at three litres per hour run for ninety seconds, with fifteen plants. Two times three is six litres per hour per plant. Six times ninety is five hundred and forty. Divide by three thousand six hundred: zero point one five litres per plant. Times fifteen plants is two point two five litres per zone. That is water delivered. To learn how much drained, measure the runoff. Neither number tells you the plant's uptake. The next lesson looks at the equipment that makes each shot happen.

visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

check.prompt: A zone was delivered 3 L, and you collected 0.6 L of runoff. What do you know about uptake?

options.text: These numbers do not measure it
options.feedback: Some water stays in the substrate or evaporates, so uptake stays unknown.

options.text: Uptake was 2.4 L
options.feedback: 2.4 L did not drain. Some stayed in the substrate and some evaporated, so uptake is unknown.

options.text: Uptake was 3 L
options.feedback: 3 L is delivery. Delivery and uptake are different things.

Multiply the per-plant litres by 18 for the zone.

options.feedback: 2 L is the total for a 20-plant zone. Per plant it is 0.1 L.

options.text: 8 L
options.feedback: 8 is the flow in L/h, not the water from a 45-second shot.

quiz.prompt: A shot gives 0.15 L per plant to 15 plants. What is the zone total?

options.feedback: Multiply per-plant water by the plant count; do not divide.
15 is the plant count, not litres. Multiply 0.15 by 15.
0.15 × 15 = 2.25 L, if every dripper gives its stated flow.

quiz.prompt: A shot equals 2% of the substrate volume. What follows?

options.text: The probe must rise exactly two points
options.feedback: Drainage, uneven spread and probe position mean the rise is often less.

options.text: The shot's volume is 2% of the substrate volume
options.feedback: That is a size guide. Read the probe for the real response.

options.text: The plant took up 2% of its daily need
options.feedback: Delivery is not uptake, and daily need was not measured.

quiz.prompt: A shot requested 120 seconds but the limit cut it to 60. Which time goes in the estimate?

options.text: 120 seconds, because it was requested
options.feedback: That would double the estimate. The shot only ran 60 seconds.

options.text: Either time; the answer is the same
options.feedback: At the same flow, half the time gives half the water.

options.text: 60 seconds, noting whether flow is rated or tested
options.feedback: Use the effective runtime and say where the flow figure came from.

lessons.title: What you need: the smallest useful system
lessons.summary: Plan one zone by five jobs: plan, measure, supply, switch and protect. Meet Home Assistant, entities and the two Crop Steering parts.
outcomes: Name the five jobs a watering system does and the equipment for each.
Explain host, Home Assistant, entity, integration, Controller and bridge in plain words.
Sketch a water path with one owner per output and a physical shutdown.

slides.title: Five jobs, one small zone
body: One zone first: prove it, then add more
Five jobs: plan · measure · supply · switch · protect
slides.narration:
In lesson A one you met the zone. It is a group of plants that get their water together, through one pipe and one on and off control. This lesson plans the equipment for one zone. Look at the single zone on this card. You build that one zone first and prove it waters correctly. Only then do you add a second. A mistake in a small system costs one zone, not a whole room.

Now picture watering by hand. You decide when and how much. You push a finger into the pot to feel how wet it is. You fill a watering can. You tip it, then stop. And you keep a towel handy for spills. An automatic system needs the same five jobs. This course calls them plan, measure, supply, switch and protect. The five labels on this card name them, and the rest of this lesson takes them one at a time.

visual.title: Five jobs, one small zone
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

check.prompt: Which of the five jobs are you doing when you fill a watering can?

options.text: Supply
options.feedback: Right. Filling the can gets water ready to deliver, which is the supply job.

options.text: Measure
options.feedback: Measuring is checking how wet the pot is, like the finger test. Filling the can is supply.

options.text: Plan
options.feedback: Planning is deciding when and how much. Filling the can is the supply job.

slides.title: Host, software and probes
body: Host = the computer that runs Home Assistant
Entity = one named reading or control
Probe → bridge, if needed → entity
slides.narration:
Start with the plan job. It needs a computer that stays switched on day and night. On that computer runs Home Assistant: free home-automation software that collects readings from sensors and switches equipment on and off. The computer that runs it is called the host. This card shows the two kinds of host the course supports. One is a Raspberry Pi, a small, low-cost computer about the size of a credit card. The other is a small PC with an Intel or AMD processor, the chip design most desktop computers use, known as x eighty-six sixty-four. You need only one.

Like a laptop, the host needs three basics, listed on this card. It needs the correct power supply, because a weak charger can make it restart at random. It needs suitable storage: the memory card or disk that holds its software and saved data. And it needs a reliable network connection to your router, the box that links your devices to each other and to the internet. The host lessons name the exact parts.

Setup has two alternative host lessons. Lesson C two A installs Home Assistant on a Raspberry Pi. Lesson C two B installs it on an x eighty-six sixty-four PC. As the card shows, both arrive at the same place: Home Assistant running and ready for the next step. Follow the lesson that matches your computer and skip the other. If someone else built the system and you only run it, you skip setup and go straight to the daily-use lessons.

Inside Home Assistant, every reading and every control gets its own name tag, like the labels on a switchboard. One tag might be a moisture reading. Another might be the on and off control for the water. Home Assistant calls each named reading or control an entity. Crop Steering joins Home Assistant through an integration: a package that teaches Home Assistant a new job. The integration stores your room settings and shows the Crop Steering screens. The Controller, the watering software from lesson B one, is a separate program. It reads those settings and entities and decides when to water. Follow the path on this card from entity to integration to Controller. You need both Crop Steering parts.

Now the measure job. Lesson A one introduced the probe, a device that measures one small spot. The moisture probe is your system's wetness check, so choose it with care. Pick a model made for your substrate. Place it in a pot that behaves like the rest of the zone. Before buying, check the maker's specification for the three items on this card. They are the exact model, its connection type, meaning how it sends readings, and the units it reports.

Some probes send their readings in a wiring language that Home Assistant cannot read on its own. They need a bridge: a small box that translates the probe's signal into one Home Assistant understands. Follow the card from the probe, through the bridge, to a Home Assistant entity. Confirm compatibility from the maker's list of supported probes for that exact bridge, rather than from matching wire colours.

EC readings need a location label too. Lesson A five named several kinds of EC, and this card compares three of them. Feed EC measures the nutrient solution in the tank. Bulk EC measures the wet substrate as a whole, water and solid together. Pore-water EC describes the water held in the pore spaces between the pieces of substrate, and it is usually estimated from bulk EC. When you choose an EC probe, read which of these it actually reports.

A reading belongs to the place where its sensor sits. The card shows a tank sensor and a root-zone sensor side by side. Suppose you rename the tank sensor's reading root-zone EC. It still measures the tank, because the name changed and the sensor did not move. Keep every label true to where its sensor really is, so later decisions use the right number.

Air readings complete the measure job. Two readings help explain why plants drink more on some days. One is air temperature. The other is relative humidity: how much moisture the air holds, compared with the most it could hold. Think of washing on a line. It dries fast on a hot, dry day and slowly on a cool, damp one. The card shows both readings feeding into water demand. Next comes the supply job: how water reaches the pots.

check.prompt: The Crop Steering screens open, but nothing decides when to water. Which part is missing?

options.text: The Controller
options.feedback: Right. The integration shows screens and stores settings; the separate Controller decides when to water.

options.text: The integration
options.feedback: The integration is what shows the screens, so it is already there. The missing decision-maker is the Controller.

slides.title: Draw the actual water path
body: A tank needs a pump; a pressurised supply may not
Add filter, regulator, drainage and backflow protection
slides.narration:
Trace the water from where it starts, the way you would follow a garden hose back to the tap. Each zone has a zone valve: a tap that opens and closes when it receives an electrical signal. Water needs pressure, meaning push, to flow out of the drippers. A pressurised supply, such as a building's water pipe, may have enough push to feed the zone valve directly. A tank of stored water usually does not. It needs a pump: a motor-driven device that pushes water along the pipe. The card shows both routes.

Many diagrams show a pump, but you add one only when your supply needs the extra push. If your route does need a pump, it also needs protection made for that pump. For example, dry-run protection switches the pump off when the tank runs empty, because a pump running without water can overheat and fail. The card pairs the pump with its protection, and the pump maker's instructions list exactly what it requires.

Now follow the rest of the path on the card. A filter catches grit that would block the drippers. A pressure regulator holds the push steady, so each dripper delivers its rated flow. A drainage path carries runoff away. Backflow protection stops water running backwards into the supply. Siphon protection stops water draining out of the tank by itself through the pipe after the pump stops. A qualified plumber confirms these parts suit your equipment and your local rules.

options.text: Yes. Every diagram shows one

slides.title: Safe switching and proof
body: Controls rated for the pump's starting load
One owner per output; an electrician does mains
Physical shutdown in reach; Watering OFF until tested
slides.narration:
Now the switch job. Control hardware is the device that turns a pump or valve on and off when the software asks. A relay is a common example: a switch operated by an electrical signal. A pump draws a burst of extra power for a moment as it starts, like the extra shove needed to get a loaded trolley rolling. That burst is called the starting load. As the card shows, choose control hardware rated for both the starting load and the running load. The big number printed on a household smart plug often describes simpler loads, such as heaters, so check its rating for motors.

Mains electricity is the high-voltage supply behind your wall sockets and switchboard, and wiring it wrongly can kill. A licensed electrician does any mains wiring for your system. This course never asks you to open or wire mains equipment, as the card reminds you. Your part is to plan, label and check.

Two people turning the same tap send mixed instructions: one opens it while the other closes it. Equipment works the same way. An output is anything the system switches, such as a pump or a valve. Give each output exactly one owner, meaning the one system allowed to switch it. The card shows one owner linked to one output. An old irrigation timer must not also switch that output.

So before the new Controller switches anything, list every system that can already switch your pump and valves. Include old timers, other home-automation rules and manual switches. Then choose one owner for each output and remove the others, following the checklist on this card.

The last job is protect, and the card shows its three parts. First, a physical shutdown: a real switch or valve, close at hand, that cuts power or water directly. Second, independent protection, such as dry-run protection, that works even if the software fails. Third, a safe place to catch test water. The Crop Steering screens also have a Watering switch, which tells the Controller whether it may start shots. Keep Watering OFF until your system passes its checks, and use the physical shutdown in an emergency, because it stops the equipment itself.

During testing, you measure what really arrives. Put collection cups under the drippers and time the run with a stopwatch, as in the catch test from lesson B four. Then send the stop command and watch the outlet. The water must physically stop. The card shows the cups, the stopwatch and the outlet.

A dashboard is the screen of readings and buttons you use to watch the system. When a dashboard icon changes to off, the software is reporting what it believes happened. To know the water really stopped, look at the outlet itself, as the card shows.

slides.title: Essentials first, extras later
body: First prove one working zone
Then add tank level, feed EC, pH, tank temperature
slides.narration: Once one zone works, extra instruments add useful information. The card lists the first ones. A tank level sensor shows how much water is left. Feed EC and pH show what is in the solution, where pH describes how acidic or alkaline it is. Tank temperature shows how warm the solution is. Later you might add more probes and a verified flow meter, which measures the water passing through the pipe. Automated nutrient dosing, thermal cameras and artificial intelligence are optional extras. Your first zone works without them. Build the basics, prove them, then add one item at a time.

body: Sketch water route, probe, Controller and shutdown

slides.narration:
Now apply all of this to your own space. On paper, sketch your water route like a simple road map. Label the supply, the pump if you need one, the zone valve, the drippers and the drainage path, in the order the water travels. The card shows that order.

Beside the water route, draw the measure and switch side. Add the probe, its bridge if it needs one, the host and the Controller. Draw a line from the Controller to each output it switches, and check that each output has only one line. Then mark the physical shutdown. The card shows both sides together.

Now circle every item you cannot name exactly, for example a pump with no model number. As the card says, each circle is a question to answer before you buy or wire anything.

Check exact models against the course's equipment and setup guide before you buy. Builders then pick a host lesson: C two A for a Raspberry Pi, or C two B for an x eighty-six sixty-four PC.

Both host routes then join the same steps, shown on this card. Install the host and both Crop Steering parts. Connect one zone's probes and outputs in the software. Prove that the water physically starts and stops. Only then add the next zone. If you only run a system someone else built, go straight to lesson D one. There you find your room and zone in the app.

slides.title: One computer keeps the system running
body: Host = the computer that runs Home Assistant
Home Assistant OS = an operating system built for it
slides.narration: Lesson C one named the host: the computer that runs Home Assistant, the software that collects readings and switches equipment. This lesson builds the host on a Raspberry Pi, the credit-card-sized computer. Lesson C two B builds it on a PC instead, and you need only one. Every computer needs an operating system: the base software that starts it and runs its programs, as Windows does on a laptop. You will install Home Assistant OS, an operating system made only to run Home Assistant. Look at the picture on screen. Readings come in, messages go out, and one always-on host sits in the middle. If you already have a working Home Assistant host, check it and skip ahead to lesson C three. Keep pumps and valves disconnected while you set up.

options.text: Complete both C2a and C2b

microSD card 32 GB+ (A2) · card reader · Ethernet cable
slides.narration: Before you start, lay the parts out on a table, as the screen shows. You need a Raspberry Pi four or Pi five with at least two gigabytes of memory, the working space it uses while running. You need a storage card: a micro S D card, the small memory card used in cameras and phones, of at least thirty-two gigabytes. The official guide suggests one marked A two, a speed rating printed on the card. You need a card reader for your everyday computer. You need the power supply made for that Pi model, because phone chargers and computer USB ports often cannot supply enough power. Last, you need an Ethernet cable: the network cable with a clip-on plug that joins the Pi to your router. The official guide requires it for installation. Check the current official guide before you buy, because its list can change.

options.feedback: Computer USB ports do not supply enough power for a Pi running Home Assistant.

slides.narration: Writing the software is different from copying a file. Home Assistant OS comes as an image: one file that is an exact copy of a ready-to-run storage card. Writing the image copies it onto your card and replaces everything already on it. The tool for this is Raspberry Pi Imager, a free program from the makers of the Pi that runs on your everyday computer. Now imagine Imager lists two places to write: a spare sixty-four gigabyte card and a one terabyte photo drive. Look at the two choices on screen. You choose the sixty-four gigabyte card, because it is the spare you checked and backed up. You leave the photo drive alone. In Imager, choose OS, then Other specific-purpose OS, then Home assistants and home automation, then Home Assistant. Pick the build for your Pi four or Pi five, then choose the checked card as storage.

slides.title: Open Home Assistant in a browser
body: Open http://homeassistant.local in a web browser
If it fails, add :8123, the Home Assistant port
slides.narration: Your everyday computer now needs to find the Pi. Every device on your network has a network address, like a house number on a street. Your web browser uses it to reach that device. Wait a few minutes after power-on. Then type homeassistant dot local into the browser, as the screen shows. If nothing opens, add colon eight one two three to the end. That number is a port: a numbered door on the host where Home Assistant answers. You can also use the Pi's numbered network address, listed in your router's settings, followed by colon eight one two three. When the page opens, check it belongs to this new Pi and not an older system. You will then see onboarding: the short set of welcome screens Home Assistant shows on its first start. Lesson C three walks through them. A working page shows the host is reachable; the probes and water get their own checks later.

slides.title: Another home for Home Assistant
body: x86-64 PC = a computer with an Intel or AMD processor
Dedicated: it does this one job. Pi OR PC, not both
slides.narration: Lesson C one named the host: the computer that runs Home Assistant, the software that collects readings and switches equipment. This lesson builds the host on an x eighty-six sixty-four PC. That is a computer with an Intel or AMD processor, the chip design most desktop computers use. Lesson C two A uses a Raspberry Pi instead, and you need only one. A popular choice is a NUC, a palm-sized box PC. Its small shape alone does not make it suitable, so the next slide checks the details. The PC must be dedicated, meaning it does this one job and nothing else. The card shows that one host is enough. If you already have a working Home Assistant host, check it and skip ahead to lesson C three. Keep pumps and valves disconnected while you set up.

visual.title: Another home for Home Assistant
visual.alt: Pi and x86-64 are alternative host routes; only one host is needed.

check.prompt: Your Raspberry Pi already runs Home Assistant well. Do you also need this PC?

options.text: No. One host is enough
options.feedback: Right. The Pi and PC routes are alternatives that reach the same place.

options.text: Yes. The PC runs the Controller
options.feedback: Both Crop Steering parts run on the one host. A second computer is not needed.

options.text: Yes. The Pi only handles readings
options.feedback: One host does every job: readings, settings and watering decisions.

slides.title: Check the computer before changing it
body: 64-bit processor · starts with UEFI · Secure Boot off
Disk with 512-byte logical sectors; back up first
slides.narration: Every computer needs an operating system: the base software that starts it and runs its programs, as Windows does on a laptop. You will install Home Assistant OS, an operating system made only to run Home Assistant. First check the exact machine against the official guide for x eighty-six sixty-four computers. Look at the three checks on this card. One, the processor must be sixty-four-bit, a design almost every PC from the last ten years has. Two, the PC must start with UEFI: the built-in startup program that runs the moment you press power. You open its settings by pressing a key during startup, and many people still call it the BIOS. There, turn off Secure Boot, a feature that only lets approved operating systems start. Three, the disk must use five-hundred-and-twelve-byte logical sectors, the size of the small blocks it stores data in. Home Assistant OS cannot start from drives that only use four-kilobyte blocks. Installing replaces everything on the disk, so back up its files and write down each setting you change.

visual.title: Check the computer before changing it

check.prompt: Two spare disks: one reports 512-byte logical sectors, the other only 4096-byte sectors. Which can hold Home Assistant OS?

options.text: The 512-byte disk
options.feedback: Right. Home Assistant OS starts only from a disk with 512-byte logical sectors.

options.text: The 4096-byte disk, because bigger blocks are faster
options.feedback: Block size is a compatibility check, not a speed choice. Home Assistant OS cannot start from it.

options.text: Either disk, if Secure Boot is off
options.feedback: Secure Boot and sector size are separate checks. Only the 512-byte disk passes.

slides.title: Example: the USB stick and the disk have different jobs
body: USB stick: runs live Ubuntu for a short while
Internal disk: receives the Home Assistant OS image
slides.narration: Picture a workbench with a borrowed toolbox and a permanent cabinet. The toolbox is a USB stick of at least eight gigabytes holding live Ubuntu. Ubuntu is a free operating system. Live means it runs straight from the USB stick without being installed, and it leaves no trace when you remove the stick. The cabinet is the PC's internal disk, which will hold Home Assistant OS for good. The card shows both jobs. Start the PC from the USB stick and choose Try Ubuntu, not Install Ubuntu. Plug in an Ethernet cable, the network cable that joins the PC to your router, so Ubuntu can reach the internet. From the official Home Assistant installation page, download the Home Assistant OS disk image: one file that is an exact copy of a ready-to-run disk. The next slide restores it onto the internal disk.

labels: Disk image: the copy to write

options.text: Try Ubuntu
options.feedback: Right. Try Ubuntu runs from the stick and changes nothing until you restore the image yourself.

options.text: Install Ubuntu
options.feedback: That would put Ubuntu on the internal disk. You only borrow Ubuntu's tools here.

options.text: Either; they do the same thing
options.feedback: Install Ubuntu writes Ubuntu to the disk. Try Ubuntu runs it from the stick only.

slides.title: Your turn: identify both devices
body: Live USB: ___. Destination disk: ___. Backup: ___.
Disks → Restore Disk Image → check target → Restore
slides.narration: Now the step that erases the disk. In Ubuntu, open Show Applications, then the program called Disks. Select the internal disk, open the three-dot menu and choose Restore Disk Image. Pick the downloaded file, then Start Restoring. Before you press the final Restore, fill in the blanks on this card. The USB stick is this device. The destination is that disk. Its backup is stored there. Identify each one by the name and capacity shown on your screen, never by a name copied from someone else's guide. If Ubuntu reports the destination is busy, you probably started from the wrong device, so fix the startup choice. When the restore finishes, shut down and remove the USB stick when Ubuntu asks. Then set UEFI to start from the internal disk.

options.feedback: Right. The internal disk is the destination. The USB stick only runs Ubuntu's tools.

options.text: The 16 GB USB stick
options.feedback: The stick is the temporary toolbox. The PC must start from its internal disk afterwards.

options.text: Both, to be safe
options.feedback: Restoring onto the stick would wipe your Ubuntu tools. Choose only the internal disk.

slides.title: A capable office PC may still be unavailable
body: Current work files are not backed up
Its owner has not agreed to dedicate it
slides.narration: Now decide for a different machine. An office PC passes every hardware check from slide two. But it still holds current work files with no backup, and its owner has not agreed to give it up. The card shows the result: capable hardware and unprotected data, so you stop before erasing. First get the owner's agreement and a working backup, or choose another suitable host. While you wait, you can keep learning in the demo, the practice copy of the app from lesson A one, which runs no equipment.

options.text: No. Only a Raspberry Pi is supported

slides.title: Finish onboarding, then read an entity ID
body: Your own account, a private recovery note, local timezone
Entity ID = exact address, like sensor.practice_moisture
slides.narration: Your host lesson ended at onboarding: the welcome screens Home Assistant shows on its first start. Complete them now. Create your own account, meaning a username and password that belong to you alone. Write down how you would get back in if you forgot the password, and keep that recovery note private and safe. Set your timezone, the local clock region, so lights-on times match the real clock. Now recall an entity: one named reading or control inside Home Assistant. Each entity has an exact written address, called an entity ID. The card shows one: sensor dot practice underscore moisture. One probe can supply several entity IDs, for example moisture, temperature and battery. The entity ID tells software where to look, and the physical label on the probe tells you where it really is.

visual.title: Finish onboarding, then read an entity ID

check.prompt: One probe reports moisture, temperature and battery level. How many entity IDs can it create?

options.text: Three, one for each reading
options.feedback: Right. Each reading gets its own entity and its own entity ID.

options.text: One for the whole probe
options.feedback: Home Assistant names each reading separately, so one probe can give several entity IDs.

options.text: None until watering starts

slides.title: Two Crop Steering parts do different jobs
body: Integration: settings + screens. Controller: when to water
Same version number for both. HACS gets the integration
slides.narration: Crop Steering arrives in two parts, as lesson C one showed. The integration is the package that adds Crop Steering to Home Assistant: it stores your room settings and shows the Crop Steering screens. The Controller is a separate program that reads those settings and decides when to water. Both parts carry one version number, and you install the same number of each. This is called version matching, and it lets each part understand the other. You get the integration from HACS, short for Home Assistant Community Store: a free extra for Home Assistant that downloads community-made integrations. HACS does not install the Controller, which comes from a different place on slide four. The card shows all three pieces. Throughout setup, keep the Watering switch OFF. Remember, that switch tells the Controller whether it may start shots.

options.text: Any version; they are independent
options.feedback: The two parts exchange settings, so they must match. Install the same number.

options.text: The oldest available version
options.feedback: An older Controller may not understand a newer integration. Match the numbers.

Open the guide's HACS link for this project and select Download. Then restart Home Assistant. Restarting closes and reopens Home Assistant's software so it loads the new part, and it takes a minute or two. Next, open the guide's Crop Steering setup link. Choose manual setup, type a room name and enter how many zones the room has. For practice, the card uses a room called Practice Room with one zone. This creates the room's record in software only. The real probes and valves are connected in lesson C four.

options.text: Installing a second host
options.feedback: One host is enough. The integration loads after a restart.

slides.title: Add and start the separate Controller
body: Add the app repository; install Crop Steering Controller
Same version · Start on boot on · Watchdog on · Watering OFF
slides.narration: The Controller installs from a different place, the app store. On Home Assistant OS, an app is a separate program that runs beside Home Assistant on the same host. The app store is the screen where you install apps, and it only lists apps from sources it knows. An app repository is a web address that adds another source to that list. Use the guide's Add the app repository link. Then install Crop Steering Controller at the same version as the integration. Review its options and start it, with Watering still OFF. The card shows two settings that keep it running. Start on boot starts the Controller whenever the host starts, and it is on by default. The Supervisor is the part of Home Assistant OS that manages apps. Watchdog, which you turn on, lets the Supervisor restart the Controller if it stops.

visual.title: Add and start the separate Controller

check.prompt: The Controller app stopped overnight while the host kept running. Which setting restarts it?

options.text: Watchdog
options.feedback: Right. With Watchdog on, the Supervisor restarts the app when it stops.

options.text: Start on boot
options.feedback: Start on boot acts only when the whole host starts. Watchdog covers an app that stops on its own.

options.text: The Watering switch
options.feedback: Watering decides whether shots may start. It does not restart the app.

slides.title: Your turn: the screens open but no heartbeat arrives
body: Heartbeat = the Controller's regular I-am-running message
Screens but no heartbeat: check the Controller app
slides.narration: Open Crop Steering in the Home Assistant sidebar, the menu down the left side of the screen. Next, check that the Controller is talking. A running Controller regularly sends Home Assistant a short status message saying it is alive. This message is called the heartbeat. Its age tells you how recently the Controller reported, as a reading's age did in lesson A six. The Controller sends it using an access key that the Supervisor hands over automatically, so you never type or paste one. Now the case on the card: the Crop Steering screens open, but no heartbeat arrives. The screens come from the integration, so check the Controller app. Is it installed, started and at the same version? If an older Controller already runs this room, finish its documented upgrade first, so that one Controller owns the room.

visual.title: Your turn: the screens open but no heartbeat arrives

check.prompt: The Crop Steering screens work, but the heartbeat age reads three hours. What does that tell you?

options.text: The Controller stopped reporting; check its app
options.feedback: Right. The screens come from the integration. An old heartbeat points at the Controller app.

options.text: The integration failed; download it again
options.feedback: The screens open, so the integration works. The heartbeat comes from the Controller.

options.text: Nothing; heartbeats only arrive during shots
options.feedback: A running Controller sends its heartbeat regularly, shots or not. Three hours old means it stopped.

slides.title: Keep a recovery copy you can actually use
body: Settings → System → Backups; keep a copy off the host
Save the emergency kit: it holds the encryption key
slides.narration: Last, make a way back. A backup is a saved copy of your Home Assistant setup that can rebuild it on new hardware. Make one in Settings, then System, then Backups. Home Assistant normally encrypts backups: it locks them with an encryption key, a long code needed to open them. It offers that key as a download called the emergency kit. As the card shows, keep the emergency kit and a backup copy away from this host. A USB stick in a drawer works. A backup kept only on the host is lost if its storage fails. Finally, compare Home Assistant's clock with your phone. Then move on to lesson C four, with Watering still OFF.

visual.title: Keep a recovery copy you can actually use

check.prompt: Your backup file is on a USB stick, but the emergency kit is lost. Can you restore it?

options.text: No. The kit holds the key that opens the backup
options.feedback: Right. An encrypted backup needs its key. Store the kit safely, away from the host.

options.text: Yes. The file alone is enough
options.feedback: An encrypted backup cannot be opened without its encryption key.

options.text: Yes, if the clock is correct
options.feedback: The clock has nothing to do with it. Opening the backup needs the key in the emergency kit.

practice.prompt: Prepare a software record with both installed version numbers, the room name, the heartbeat age, how you would recover your account, and where the backup copy and emergency kit are kept.
hints: HACS download, room setup and the Controller app install are separate steps.
An encrypted backup needs its emergency kit to open.
practice.success: The record shows matching version numbers, the intended room, a fresh heartbeat, an account-recovery method and an off-host backup with its emergency kit.

quiz.prompt: What does HACS download in this course's route?

options.text: The integration; the Controller comes from the app store
options.feedback: Right. HACS, the setup link and the app store are three separate steps.

options.text: Both parts and every connected device
options.feedback: HACS gets only the integration. The Controller comes from the app store, and devices are added separately.

options.text: Firmware for every sensor
options.feedback: HACS downloads Home Assistant integrations. Probe firmware comes from the probe maker.

quiz.prompt: The Crop Steering screens open, but there is no fresh heartbeat. What next?

options.text: Check the Controller is installed, started and the same version, with Watering OFF
options.feedback: Right. The screens come from the integration; the heartbeat comes from the Controller.

options.text: Turn Watering ON to force a heartbeat
options.feedback: Watering does not start a stopped app, and it must stay OFF until checks pass.

options.text: Assume the screens prove the Controller works
options.feedback: The screens come from the integration. Only a fresh heartbeat shows the Controller is running.

quiz.prompt: What is an entity ID?

options.text: The exact written address of one reading or control
options.feedback: Right. Check its units and the probe's physical label separately.

options.text: Proof that a valve is wired correctly
options.feedback: An entity ID is a software address. Wiring is checked physically.

options.text: The serial number of a whole device
options.feedback: One device can have several entity IDs, one per reading or control.

quiz.prompt: The only backup is on the host's storage, which just failed. Can you recover?

options.text: No. You need a copy off the host and its emergency kit
options.feedback: Right. Keep a backup copy and the emergency kit somewhere other than the host.

options.text: Yes. A screenshot of the finished backup is enough
options.feedback: A screenshot is not the backup file. Recovery needs the file and its key.

options.text: Yes. Setting the timezone restores the files
options.feedback: The timezone sets the clock. It does not restore anything.

slides.title: A contact name needs the right number
body: Mapping = telling Crop Steering which entities a zone uses
Add devices to Home Assistant first; then Equipment → Setup
slides.narration: A phone contact can have the right name and still dial the wrong number. Software works the same way. Mapping means telling Crop Steering which Home Assistant entities belong to each zone: this probe, this valve. First add each probe and valve control to Home Assistant through its own supported setup, because Crop Steering only maps entities that already exist. Check each entity ID, the exact written address from lesson C three, against the physical label on the equipment, as the card shows. Then open Crop Steering, select the room, and open the Equipment menu, then Setup. Keep the Watering switch OFF, so the Controller starts no shots, and keep the physical shutdowns your installer set up in place.

visual.alt: Actual isolated demo screen. Read the displayed room and current sample values; separate paper examples use fictional values.

check.prompt: A new probe is not in Home Assistant yet. Can you map it in Crop Steering?

options.text: No. Add it to Home Assistant first
options.feedback: Right. Setup maps entities that already exist; it does not add devices.

options.text: Yes. Setup finds and adds it
options.feedback: Setup only lists existing entities. Add the probe through its own Home Assistant setup first.

options.text: Yes, after turning Watering ON
options.feedback: Watering stays OFF, and it does not add devices. Add the probe to Home Assistant first.

slides.title: Match the real plumbing and measurements
body: Supply type: Zone valves only OR A pump, then zone valves
Probes: VWC in percent, recent last update, EC type known
slides.narration: Setup asks how water reaches the room, called the supply type. Choose Zone valves only when each zone valve is fed straight from a pressurised supply. Choose A pump, then zone valves when water flows only while a pump runs. Map a pump only if one really exists, and give every zone its own valve. Then look at the probes, as on this screen. Check two things for each moisture probe. First the units: VWC should read in percent. Second the last update: the time of its newest reading, which should be recent. For each EC probe, note whether it gives feed, bulk or pore-water EC. If an optional reading does not exist, leave it unmapped rather than borrowing another number.

visual.title: Match the real plumbing and measurements
visual.alt: Actual isolated demo screen. Read the displayed room and current sample values; separate paper examples use fictional values.

check.prompt: A small room has one zone valve fed straight from a building's water pipe. There is no pump. Which supply type?

options.text: Zone valves only
options.feedback: Right. The pressurised supply feeds the valve directly, so no pump is mapped.

options.text: A pump, then zone valves
options.feedback: That type needs a real pump to map. This room has none.

options.text: Leave the supply type blank
options.feedback: Setup needs the answer and does not guess. Choose Zone valves only.

slides.title: Example: twelve plants, not one giant pot
body: 12 plants · 3 L substrate per plant · 2 drippers per plant
3 L/h per dripper → 12 × 2 × 3 = 72 L/h zone delivery
slides.narration: Next comes sizing: the numbers that turn runtime into litres. Setup asks for four numbers per zone, and all except the plant count are per plant. Imagine twelve plants, each in three litres of substrate, each with two drippers measured at three litres per hour. Enter plant count twelve, substrate per plant three litres, drippers per plant two, and flow per dripper three litres per hour. The card shows the zone delivery. Twelve plants times two drippers is twenty-four drippers. Twenty-four times three litres per hour is seventy-two litres per hour. Keep the per-plant box at three litres, not thirty-six. Thirty-six litres is the zone's total substrate, and it would tell the software each plant has a giant pot.

visual.title: Example: twelve plants, not one giant pot

workedExample.prompt: Estimate delivery for 12 plants with 2 drippers each, measured at 3 L/h per dripper.
steps: 12 × 2 = 24 drippers.
24 × 3 = 72 L/h estimated zone delivery.
Enter substrate as 3 L per plant, not the 36 L total.
workedExample.answer: 72 L/h zone delivery. It describes water supplied, not water taken up by the plants.

check.prompt: Six plants each sit in 4 L of substrate. What goes in substrate per plant?

options.text: 4 L
options.feedback: Right. The box is per plant. The software multiplies by the plant count itself.
24 L is the zone total, 6 × 4. The box asks for one plant's substrate.

options.text: 6 L
options.feedback: 6 is the plant count. Enter each plant's substrate, 4 L.

slides.title: Check the clock and the receipt
body: Lights-on and lights-off hours must match the real timer
Review → Save → wait for Mapping acknowledged
slides.narration: Two checks come before saving. First the clock. Write down the timezone, the room's lights-on and lights-off hours in Crop Steering, and the times on the real light timer. They must agree, because Crop Steering does not switch the lights; it only uses those hours to plan the day. Second, the receipt. Choose Review configuration, read the list of changes and problems, then choose Save configuration. Each save creates a new revision: a numbered edition of the setup. Saving is like posting a letter. The Controller then reads the new revision and sends back an acknowledgement, its receipt, which the card shows as Mapping acknowledged. Wait for that receipt for this revision. A fresh heartbeat shows the Controller is alive, and only the acknowledgement shows it accepted your setup.

visual.title: Check the clock and the receipt

check.prompt: Setup was saved a minute ago. The heartbeat is fresh, but Mapping acknowledged has not appeared. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for the acknowledgement, with Watering OFF
options.feedback: Right. Saved and accepted are separate. Only the receipt shows the Controller took this revision.

options.text: Treat the fresh heartbeat as the receipt
options.feedback: The heartbeat says the Controller is alive, not that it accepted this revision.

options.text: Turn Watering ON to speed it up
options.feedback: Watering stays OFF. It does not make the Controller accept a revision.

slides.title: Your turn: three faults in one record
body: 8 × 1 × 2.5 = 20 L/h: the arithmetic is right
Faults: wrong-room probe, blank lights hours, no receipt
slides.narration: Now review a record yourself. Eight plants, four litres per plant, one dripper each, measured at two point five litres per hour. Eight plants times one dripper is eight drippers. Eight times two point five litres per hour is twenty litres per hour. The arithmetic is right, but the card shows three faults. The moisture entity belongs to the next room. The lights-on and lights-off hours are blank. And the revision is saved but not acknowledged. Each fault must be fixed before Watering can be turned on. You can practise this kind of review in the demo, with no equipment connected.

visual.title: Your turn: three faults in one record

check.prompt: Ten plants have two drippers each, measured at 1.5 L/h per dripper. What is the zone delivery?

options.text: 30 L/h
options.feedback: Right. 10 × 2 = 20 drippers, and 20 × 1.5 = 30 L/h.

options.text: 15 L/h
options.feedback: That uses one dripper per plant. Multiply by 2 drippers first: 20 × 1.5 = 30 L/h.

options.text: 3 L/h
options.feedback: That is two drippers on one plant. Multiply by all 10 plants: 30 L/h.

slides.title: Read the accepted setup back
body: Check Overview → Selected room and Equipment → Probes
Unknown is not OFF. Watering stays OFF until C5 and C6
slides.narration: After the acknowledgement arrives, read the setup back. Open Overview, the main status screen, then Selected room, its view of one room. Next open Equipment, then Probes. Compare each reading, its units and its age with your written setup sheet. Check the sizing, the measured flow, the light hours and the one owner of each output. A state that reads unknown means the software cannot tell, so treat it as a fault to fix, not as OFF. The card shows the accepted revision and the live values. Lesson C five checks the physical protections, and lesson C six proves the water starts and stops. Until those pass with the responsible people present, Watering stays OFF.

options.feedback: Right. Unknown means the software cannot tell. Find out why before going further.

options.text: As OFF, since nothing is running
options.feedback: Unknown is not a reading of OFF. The valve could be in any state.

options.text: As ON, to be careful
options.feedback: Guessing either way hides the fault. Fix the reading so the state is known.

options.feedback: Right. The entity ID must match the physical probe in this zone.

options.text: Use it because the name sounds right

options.text: Average it with the tank temperature

options.text: 20 L/h
options.feedback: 20 is the dripper count. Multiply by 2 L/h each: 40 L/h.

quiz.prompt: The Home Assistant timezone is correct. What still needs checking?

options.text: The room's lights hours against the real light timer
options.feedback: Right. Crop Steering plans by those hours but does not switch the lights.

options.text: Nothing; the timezone sets every light
options.feedback: The timezone sets the clock. The lights follow their own timer.

options.text: Only the browser theme
options.feedback: The theme changes colours. The lights hours must match the real timer.

quiz.prompt: Setup is saved and the heartbeat is fresh, but there is no Mapping acknowledged. Ready to water?

options.text: No. Keep Watering OFF until the acknowledgement arrives
options.feedback: Right. Saved and accepted are separate states. Wait for the receipt.

options.text: Yes. Saved and accepted mean the same
options.feedback: Saving stores the setup. Only the acknowledgement shows the Controller took it.

options.text: Yes. Watering will force acceptance
