lessons.title: Make the physical equipment safe to test
lessons.summary: Learn what the Watering switch can and cannot stop, check how each probe and pump is connected, and give every output one controller before any water flows.
outcomes: Explain why Watering OFF is a software block, not physical isolation
Check a probe's supply voltage, signal protocol, firmware and interface against its documentation
Record ratings, protections, physical shutdown and one owner for every output before the wet test

slides.title: Watering OFF is a software block, not isolation
body: Watering OFF: the Controller starts no shots
Isolation: power and water cut off by real devices
Agree the physical shutdown and who controls it
slides.narration: Think of a stop request to a bus driver. Only that driver hears it. Crop Steering’s Watering switch works like that request. Each room has a Watering switch at the top of its screen, and you have kept it OFF since lesson C three. When Watering is OFF, the Controller starts no shots in that room. That includes rescue shots and test shots. A test shot is a shot you ask the app to run on demand. A shot that is already running stops within a few seconds. That is a software block. It does not cut electricity, and it cannot stop an old timer or a hand switch. Physical isolation means cutting power or water with a real device. Examples are a switch that cuts the electricity supply, or a closed hand valve on the water line. Electrical isolation is the power part of that. Look at the cues on screen. Before anyone works on a pump, valve or wiring, agree the approved electrical and water shutdown, and who controls it. Next, you check how each probe connects.

visual.title: A stop message is not a disconnected machine

check.prompt: Watering is OFF for Room A. An old timer is still wired to the Zone 1 valve. What can still open that valve?

options.text: The old timer
options.feedback: Right. Watering OFF only stops the Crop Steering Controller. The timer is a separate route to water.

options.text: Nothing; Watering OFF blocks every device
options.feedback: Watering OFF blocks Controller shots only. Timers and hand switches still work.

options.text: Only a Crop Steering rescue shot
options.feedback: Watering OFF blocks rescue shots too. The timer is the route that remains.

slides.title: Use the probe’s documented connection
body: Check supply voltage, signal protocol, firmware, interface
Never guess a wire’s job from its colour
First install: choose a documented, assembled route
slides.narration: A plug that fits is like an envelope that fits a letterbox. The letter inside can still be wrong. So you check four things before you connect a probe. Supply voltage is the electrical push the probe needs to run, measured in volts. Too much can destroy it. The signal protocol is the wiring language from lesson C one: how the probe sends its readings. The interface is whatever the probe plugs into. Often that is a bridge, the translator box. The interface must speak the probe’s language. Firmware is the small program built into the probe or bridge. Some probes need a particular firmware version. Look at the cues on screen. For example, before you connect a TEROS twelve, read its maker’s sheet. Confirm its voltage, protocol and the bridges it supports. Then follow its placement and calibration steps. Never guess a wire’s job from its colour, and never connect an unknown signal straight to the metal pins on a computer board. For a first install, choose a documented, assembled route. Next, check that a working reading measures the right thing.

visual.title: Use the probe’s documented connection

check.prompt: A new probe’s plug fits your bridge, but its sheet lists a supply voltage the bridge does not provide. What do you do?

options.text: Stop and find an interface the probe’s documents support
options.feedback: Right. A fitting plug says nothing about voltage or protocol. Use a documented match.

options.text: Connect it, because the plug fits
options.feedback: Plugs can fit while the voltage is wrong. The wrong voltage can destroy the probe.

options.text: Swap wires by colour until a reading appears
options.feedback: Colours do not define a wire’s job. Guessing can damage the probe or the bridge.

slides.title: Example: a number can be fresh and irrelevant
body: Fresh 22 °C tank reading is not zone moisture
Check quantity, units, real location and age together
Bulk EC does not become pore-water EC by renaming
slides.narration: A reading can be recent and still answer the wrong question. Picture a thermometer hanging in the tank, not in the pot. Here is a made-up example. Remember: an entity is one named reading or control inside Home Assistant. This entity shows twenty-two. It updated two minutes ago, so it is fresh. Its name mentions Room A. But its unit is degrees Celsius, and the sensor sits in the tank. Moisture in Room A is VWC, a percentage of the substrate’s volume, measured in the pot. So this number cannot stand in for moisture. Look at the three labels on screen. Check four things together: quantity, units, real location and age. The same care applies to EC. Remember from lesson A five: bulk EC is measured through the substrate. Pore-water EC describes the water between the pieces. A bulk EC reading does not become pore-water EC because a field asks for it. A wrong reading makes the Controller water for the wrong reason. Next, look at the pump.

visual.alt: Actual isolated demo screen. Read the displayed room and current sample values; separate paper examples use fictional values.

Location: the tank, not the substrate in Room A’s pots.
Choose the verified moisture entity from the probe in the pot instead.

check.prompt: An entity named Room A EC reads 1.8 mS/cm, updated a minute ago. It measures the feed tank. Can it fill Room A’s pore-water EC field?

options.text: No; it measures feed in the tank, not water in the pot
options.feedback: Right. Location and method matter. Feed EC is not pore-water EC.

options.text: Yes; the units are mS/cm
options.feedback: Matching units do not make the same measurement. Check where and how it was measured.

options.text: Yes; it is fresh
options.feedback: Freshness shows the reading is recent. It does not show what or where it measures.

slides.title: Check what starts and stops the pump
body: Pumps draw a surge at start-up: the starting load
A competent installer checks ratings and protection
Plan for dry-run, deadheading, backflow and siphon
slides.narration: Remember from lesson C one: a pump draws a burst of extra power as it starts, like the shove that gets a loaded trolley rolling. That burst is the starting load. A rating is the most a device is designed to handle safely. It is printed on its label. A smart plug’s headline rating usually describes a heater, not a motor. A competent installer is a qualified person, such as a licensed electrician or plumber. That person checks the real pump, its control hardware, the ratings and the protection it needs. Mains is the high-voltage power behind your wall sockets, and this course gives no mains-wiring instructions. The installer also plans for faults. Dry-run means the pump runs with no water and overheats. Deadheading means the pump pushes against a closed valve, with nowhere for water to go. Backflow and siphon, from lesson C one, mean water running backwards or draining on its own. Look at the cues on screen. Before any test, agree what will be energised, meaning receive power, where water comes out, and how the test ends. Next, find any second controller.

visual.title: Check what starts and stops the pump

check.prompt: Your pump runs from a smart plug whose label gives a rating for heaters. Is that label enough to approve it for the pump?

options.text: No; a competent installer checks the motor’s starting load
options.feedback: Right. A heater rating does not cover a motor’s start-up burst. The installer decides.

options.text: Yes; the pump is small, so any plug will do
options.feedback: Even a small motor draws a burst at start-up. Only an installer can approve the match.

options.text: Yes, if the dashboard shows it switching
options.feedback: A switching icon proves communication, not a safe electrical rating.

slides.title: Your turn: two controllers know the same valve
body: Old timer can still open the valve
Watering OFF does not stop the timer
Give each output one owner before testing
slides.narration: Two people steering one car is dangerous, even when one of them is resting. A valve works the same way. Here is the case. An old timer is still wired to a valve. You have also mapped that valve into Crop Steering, and Watering is OFF. Remember from lesson C four: mapping tells Crop Steering which entity is which valve. The old timer is a competing controller, a second system that can also open the valve. Look at the comparison on screen. The left side can still act. The right side is OFF, but that does not stop the left. So the valve is not isolated. Write down both routes to water. Then choose one owner for the output, and have the installer disable or remove the other route. Crop Steering may still do read-only observation. That means it reads values but sends no commands. Agree how the plants still get water while you sort this out. Two owners can fight, double-water or leave a valve open. Next, close the physical checks.

visual.title: Your turn: two controllers know the same valve
visual.alt: The old timer and new Controller must not both own an output.

check.prompt: An older Home Assistant automation also switches your Zone 1 valve. Crop Steering will own it. What happens before testing?

options.text: Disable or remove the automation so one controller owns the valve
options.feedback: Right. One owner per output. The old automation could open the valve at any time.

options.text: Keep both; the faster one wins
options.feedback: Two controllers can fight or double-water. Remove one route first.

options.text: Leave it; Watering OFF overrides it
options.feedback: Watering OFF only blocks Crop Steering. The automation still works.

slides.title: Close the physical checks before the wet test
body: Trace each probe and each output to real equipment
Record ratings, protections, owner and shutdown
Go to C6 only with an approved catch-test plan
slides.narration: Before you leave a house, you check the doors, the oven and the taps. This slide is that last walk round. A wet test is the first time water really flows through the new system. First, trace each probe to its Home Assistant reading. Then trace each control entity back to the real valve or pump. Where the design allows, the installer confirms each output with a low-risk indicator, such as a small lamp, in place of the real load. Never use a live crop as the first wiring test. Look at the three cues on screen. Then write the setup record: interface, ratings, protections, one owner and the physical shutdown. For example: Zone one valve, owned by Crop Steering, old timer removed, water shutdown at the labelled hand valve. An open question keeps this stage unfinished. Move to lesson C six only with an approved catch-test method and safe collection ready. Lesson C six runs that first careful water test.

visual.title: Close the physical checks before the wet test

check.prompt: Your record lists probes, ratings and owners, but the physical shutdown line is blank. Can you start C6?

options.text: No; agree and record the physical shutdown first
options.feedback: Right. Everyone must know how to stop real water and power before it flows.

options.text: Yes; the Watering switch is the shutdown
options.feedback: Watering OFF is a software block. A physical shutdown cuts real power or water.

options.text: Yes; fill it in after the test
options.feedback: You need the shutdown during the test, in case water does not stop.

lessons.title: First water: catch it, measure it, stop it
lessons.summary: Commission one zone in two stages: an installer-run equipment test with Watering OFF, then a supervised Controller cycle once every readiness check passes.

Turn a timed catch in millilitres into litres per hour, and spot uneven delivery
Use the readiness checklist, then supervise and record the first enabled cycle

slides.title: Two tests answer two questions
body: Commissioning: prove each part works before relying on it
Stage one: equipment test, Watering stays OFF
Stage two: supervised Controller cycle, after readiness
slides.narration: Before a new building opens, someone checks the pipes and the wiring. For your system, that check is called commissioning. It means proving each part works safely before you rely on it. It has two stages. Look at the cues on screen. Stage one is the equipment test. It asks: does water go where it should, and does it stop? Stage two is the supervised Controller cycle. It asks: does Crop Steering water correctly on its own while someone watches? In stage one, the Watering switch stays OFF. Remember from lesson C five: OFF blocks every Controller shot, test shots included. So the competent installer runs the valve or pump with the maker’s approved procedure. The test has a bounded duration, meaning a fixed length of time agreed in advance. For example, thirty seconds, with cups under the drippers and the physical shutdown within reach. Next, watch the whole water path.

visual.title: Two tests answer two questions

check.prompt: Stage one is about to start. Someone suggests turning Watering ON to fire a test shot. What is right?

options.text: Keep Watering OFF; the installer runs the approved equipment procedure
options.feedback: Right. Stage one tests the water path itself, with the Controller blocked.

options.text: Turn Watering ON briefly, since it is only a test
options.feedback: Watering ON lets the Controller start any shot that is due, rescue shots included. That is stage two.

options.text: Work round the Watering switch in Home Assistant
options.feedback: Never bypass the block. Ask the installer for an approved equipment procedure instead.

slides.title: Watch the whole water path
body: Remove only the isolation this test needs
One catch cup per dripper, timed with a stopwatch
Watch the drippers until the water really stops
slides.narration: Picture filling a bath while you check every other tap in the house. You want one tap running and no others. With the installer present, remove only the isolation this one test needs. Leave everything else shut off. Look at the diagram on screen. Water flows from the supply, through the valve, to the drippers. Remember from lesson B four: a dripper is a small tap at each plant. Place a catch cup, a small measuring cup, under several drippers. Use one cup per dripper, not one cup for all. Time the run with a stopwatch. While it runs, watch three things. The intended drippers should flow. Other zones should stay dry. The pump and valve should switch in the agreed order. Then stop the test the agreed way, and keep watching the drippers until the water stops. Also check for siphon, from lesson C one: water that keeps draining after the stop. A screen icon reports what the software sent, so your eyes on the dripper are the proof. Next, turn a cup into a number.

visual.title: Watch the whole water path
visual.alt: Timed individual catches, observed stopping and a checked water path.

check.prompt: After the stop, the valve icon turns grey, but one dripper keeps dribbling for a minute. What do you record?

options.text: Water did not stop; investigate siphon or the valve before going on
options.feedback: Right. The dripper is the evidence. Find the cause and retest.

options.text: Stopped, because the icon is grey
options.feedback: The icon shows the command sent. The dripper shows what the water did.

options.text: Nothing; one minute is too short to matter
options.feedback: Water that keeps flowing after a stop is a fault. It can overwater or drain a tank.

slides.title: Example: a cup becomes a flow measurement
body: Separate cups: 30, 33, 37 mL = 3.6, 3.96, 4.44 L/h
slides.narration: A cup tells you millilitres in a number of seconds. Your setup from lesson C four asks for litres per hour, written L slash h. Here is how to convert, step by step. Suppose one dripper fills its cup with thirty millilitres in thirty seconds. Step one: change millilitres to litres. Thirty divided by one thousand is zero point zero three litres. Step two: scale up to an hour. An hour has three thousand six hundred seconds. Zero point zero three times three thousand six hundred is one hundred and eight. Step three: divide by the thirty seconds the test ran. One hundred and eight divided by thirty is three point six. So this dripper delivers three point six litres per hour. Look at the three steps on screen. Now say three cups held thirty, thirty-three and thirty-seven millilitres. They work out to three point six, three point nine six and four point four four litres per hour. One total would hide that difference. These are example numbers, so never enter them for a real zone. Next, you try one yourself.

visual.title: Example: a cup becomes a flow measurement

workedExample.prompt: Convert 30 mL caught in 30 seconds into L/h.
steps: 108 ÷ 30 s of runtime = 3.6.
Record the dripper, runtime and test conditions beside the result.
workedExample.answer: 3.6 L/h for that dripper during this catch.

check.prompt: A dripper fills its cup with 25 mL in 30 seconds. What is its flow?

options.text: 25 L/h
options.feedback: That skips the conversion. Change mL to litres, scale to an hour, then divide by seconds.
25 ÷ 30 gives mL per second. You still need to scale to an hour and convert to litres.

slides.title: Your turn: finish the catch record
body: Uneven delivery: find the cause, fix it, catch again
Never fake a fault by pulling wires or power
slides.narration: Now you try it. A dripper fills twenty-four millilitres in thirty seconds. Pause and work it out. Twenty-four divided by one thousand is zero point zero two four litres. Times three thousand six hundred is eighty-six point four. Divided by thirty is two point eight eight litres per hour. Write that on the record with the dripper, the runtime and the conditions. Look at the cues on screen. Suppose its neighbours gave about three point six. That gap is uneven delivery, meaning some plants get less water than others. Look for a clog, a leak or low pressure. Fix it, then repeat the catch. Then the installer tests the independent protections, such as dry-run protection, with the maker’s method. Remember from lesson C five: deadheading means a pump pushing against a closed valve. Never fake a fault by pulling wires or power while the pump runs, or by shutting valves against it. That can wreck the pump or flood the room. Next, decide whether a good catch is enough.

visual.title: Your turn: finish the catch record

check.prompt: Four drippers measure 3.6, 3.5, 3.7 and 1.9 L/h. What do you do?

options.text: Inspect the 1.9 L/h dripper, fix it and repeat the catch
options.feedback: Right. That plant gets about half the water. Find the clog, leak or pressure fault.

options.text: Average the four and move on
options.feedback: An average hides the plant that is short of water. Investigate the low dripper.

options.text: Lengthen the runtime for the whole zone
options.feedback: That overwaters the other plants and leaves the fault in place. Fix the cause.

slides.title: A good catch is one part of readiness
body: Readiness checklist: every item must pass
Saved but not acknowledged: keep Watering OFF
Enter measured flow, then wait for the receipt
slides.narration: A pilot runs a whole checklist, not only the fuel check. Your system needs the same. The readiness checklist is the list of checks that must all pass before stage two. Look at the cues on screen. The items are: correct room and outputs, fresh probe readings and acknowledged mapping. Then measured flow, water seen stopping and tested protections. Then lights-on and lights-off hours, timezone, approved local targets and recovery access. Remember from lesson C four: acknowledgement is the Controller’s receipt for a saved setup. Now decide a case. The catch and the stop both passed. You entered the measured flow and pressed Save configuration. But Mapping acknowledged has not appeared. Keep Watering OFF. Find out why the Controller has not accepted the revision, fix it and wait for the receipt. Turning Watering on will not repair a setup problem. Next, the first supervised cycle.

visual.title: A good catch is one part of readiness

check.prompt: Every readiness item passes except the room’s lights-on and lights-off hours, which are blank. Can stage two start?

options.text: No; enter and check the hours against the real lights first
options.feedback: Right. The phases follow lights-on and lights-off. Blank hours mean wrong timing.

options.text: Yes; lighting does not affect watering
options.feedback: It does. From B2, each phase is timed from lights-on and lights-off.

options.text: Yes; the catch test passed
options.feedback: A good catch is one item. Every item must pass.

slides.title: Supervise the first enabled cycle
body: Operator turns Watering ON for the selected room
Watch the shot, the stop and the event record
Water won’t stop: physical shutdown first, then OFF
slides.narration: A learner driver’s first trip has an instructor in the next seat. Stage two is that first trip. Once every readiness item passes, the responsible operator turns Watering ON for the selected room. Enabling Watering lets Crop Steering start any shot it decides is due, including rescue shots. So this is real watering, not a harmless check. Use approved local settings, not this course’s example numbers. Keep the catch cups and the shutdown ready. Look at the cues on screen. Watch the right drippers run, other zones stay dry and the water stop. Then check the event record, which lists shots that happened. Check the next action, the Controller’s note of what it plans next. If water keeps flowing when it should not, use the physical shutdown first. Then turn Watering OFF. Write down what happened and the agreed final state, for example Watering ON, with the operator checking each shot today. Repeat both stages for each new output. After the quiz, lesson C seven shows how to move zones over from an older controller, one at a time.

visual.title: Supervise the first enabled cycle

check.prompt: During stage two, a valve keeps running after the shot should have ended. What do you do first?

options.text: Use the physical shutdown, then turn Watering OFF
options.feedback: Right. Stop the real water first. Then block the Controller and investigate.

options.text: Turn Watering OFF and wait to see
options.feedback: Watering OFF is a software block. If the valve is stuck, only the physical shutdown stops water.

options.text: Lower the moisture target
options.feedback: Targets change future decisions. They do not stop water already flowing.

practice.prompt: Calculate the flow for 18 mL caught in 20 seconds. Then review a setup that is saved but not acknowledged, and write your stage-two decision and final-state record.
hints: 18 mL = 0.018 L. Multiply by 3600, then divide by 20 seconds.
Stage two needs acknowledged mapping as well as every physical and software readiness item.
practice.success: 0.018 × 3600 ÷ 20 = 3.24 L/h. Keep Watering OFF until Mapping acknowledged appears. Record the real delivery, the observed stop and the agreed final state.

quiz.prompt: Watering is OFF. Can a Crop Steering test shot run for stage one?

options.text: No; stage one uses the installer’s approved equipment procedure
options.feedback: Right. OFF blocks ordinary, rescue and test shots. Never bypass it.

options.text: Yes; test shots ignore Watering OFF
options.feedback: Test shots are blocked too. That is why the installer runs stage one.

options.text: Yes; the demo’s test button runs the real valve
options.feedback: The demo is a practice copy that runs no equipment.

quiz.prompt: A dripper fills its cup with 40 mL in 40 seconds. What is its flow?

options.text: 40 L/h
options.feedback: That skips the conversion. Change mL to litres, multiply by 3600, then divide by 40.

options.text: 1 L/h
options.feedback: 40 ÷ 40 is mL per second. Scale to an hour and convert: 1 mL/s = 3.6 L/h.

quiz.prompt: The screen says OFF, but water keeps flowing. What do you do?

options.text: Use the agreed physical shutdown, then find the fault
options.feedback: Right. Real flowing water outranks what a screen says.

options.text: Wait for the icon to change again
options.feedback: Waiting lets water keep flowing. Stop it physically first.

options.text: Lower the moisture target
options.feedback: A target changes future shots. It cannot stop water already flowing.

quiz.prompt: When may the first supervised stage-two cycle begin?

options.text: After every software and physical readiness item passes
options.feedback: Right. Then the operator enables Watering with approved settings, supervision and shutdown ready.

options.text: As soon as one catch succeeds
options.feedback: A catch is one item. Mapping, readings, timing, targets and protections must pass too.

options.text: When the Crop Steering workspace opens
options.feedback: An open page shows the software runs. It proves nothing about water or setup.

slides.title: Moving house starts with a labelled inventory
body: Growlink: an existing commercial irrigation controller
Migration: moving control from one system to another
Start by observing one room and one zone
slides.narration: Before you move house, you label every box while it is still in the old house. This lesson is about that kind of move. Growlink is a commercial irrigation controller sold by another company. Some growers already water with it. Migration means moving control of your watering from one system to another, here from Growlink to Crop Steering. If you have no Growlink system, follow along on paper. Look at the cues on screen. First, observe and change nothing. Pick one room and one zone. Write down its probes, valves, pump and the controller in charge today. Also write who runs it and who can recover it if it fails. For example: Room A, Zone one, one moisture probe, one valve, shared pump, owned by Growlink, run by the head grower. A working Growlink probe may still be unable to connect to Home Assistant. The current operator keeps caring for the crop while you plan. Next, keep the old records safe.

visual.title: Moving house starts with a labelled inventory

check.prompt: You want to move Room A from Growlink to Crop Steering. What do you do first?

options.text: Record one zone’s equipment, settings and owner without changing anything
options.feedback: Right. A clear record of today’s setup is your starting point and your way back.

options.text: Switch Growlink off for the whole room
options.feedback: The plants would lose their water, and you lose the working baseline.

options.text: Plug the Growlink probes into Home Assistant
options.feedback: Compatibility is unknown. Check each probe’s documents first, as in C5.

slides.title: Keep the records in their original context
body: Use exports your account offers, or copy by hand
Keep original files, dates, units and timezone
The same label in two systems can mean different things
slides.narration: Photos of the old house help you set up the new one. Old records do the same job here. An export is a file a program saves so you can open the data somewhere else, such as a spreadsheet. Some products also offer an API, a doorway that lets other software fetch data automatically. Use only what your own Growlink account actually shows. If it offers neither, copy settings and history by hand or with screenshots. Keep the original files and their dates unchanged. Look at the cues on screen. Write down the timezone, lights-on and lights-off times, and substrate per plant. Add plant and dripper counts, measured flow, targets and how each value was measured. For example, a value labelled EC needs a note of where it was measured: tank, runoff or substrate. Crop Steering does not read Growlink files. You will enter checked values yourself on the Setup screen from lesson C four. Next, match old names to real equipment.

visual.title: Keep the records in their original context

check.prompt: An old Growlink record says EC 2.4, with no note of where it was measured. What do you write beside it?

options.text: Method unknown; find out before using it
options.feedback: Right. Feed, runoff and substrate EC are different measurements. Record the gap.

options.text: Pore-water EC
options.feedback: That is a guess. A wrong label could feed the Controller the wrong kind of EC.

options.text: Feed EC, because most records are
options.feedback: Still a guess. Check the original setup or ask the person who ran it.

slides.title: Example: one old zone, several new addresses
body: Old label: Room A, Zone 1
Same friendly name does not prove the same device
Write exact new entity IDs beside the old record
slides.narration: A contact called Mum on a new phone is only useful if the number is right. Names in two systems work the same way. Each Home Assistant entity has a friendly name, the readable label people see, such as Room A Zone one valve. It also has an entity ID, the exact address software uses, from lesson C three. Imagine Growlink calls a valve Room A, Zone one. Your Home Assistant now has an entity with that same friendly name. That match proves nothing about the real device. Someone may have typed the label onto the wrong valve. Look at the cues on screen. Trace the actual valve and probe with the installer. Confirm the interface, units and data age, as in lesson C five. Write the exact new entity ID beside the old record. Mark anything you cannot confirm as unknown. Then use lesson C four’s mapping and sizing checks to enter values. Old targets may mean something different in Crop Steering’s fields. Next, plan the handover.

visual.title: Example: one old zone, several new addresses

workedExample.prompt: Does a matching valve name prove the zone is ready to move?
steps: Keep the original Growlink room and zone record.
Trace the physical valve and write its exact new entity ID.
Confirm compatible control and one owner before commissioning.
workedExample.answer: No. A matching friendly name proves neither the real device nor who controls it.

check.prompt: switch.zone_1_valve has the friendly name Room A Zone 1. What proves it is the real Zone 1 valve?

options.text: Tracing it to the physical valve with the installer
options.feedback: Right. Only a physical trace links an entity to real equipment.

options.text: The friendly name matches the Growlink label
options.feedback: Anyone can type any label. A name is not a physical check.

options.text: It updated a minute ago
options.feedback: Fresh data shows communication, not which valve it controls.

slides.title: Agree the handover and the way back
body: Handover: the moment a zone changes controller
One controller per output, before and after
Rollback: checked steps back to the old setup
slides.narration: When a night nurse hands over to a day nurse, they agree the exact moment. Only one is in charge at a time. A handover is that moment for a zone, when control of its valve moves from Growlink to Crop Steering. Plan it with the responsible operator and the installer. Agree the time, which old controls get disabled, and how the plants get water during the work. Look at the diagram on screen. Each physical output has one controller at a time. Crop Steering may observe read-only, as in lesson C five, but it must never command a valve that Growlink still runs. Also write a rollback. A rollback is a checked set of steps to put the old arrangement back if a check fails. For example: make sure Crop Steering can no longer run Zone one, re-enable its Growlink schedule, then watch one shot start and stop. A rollback never means leaving both schedules running in case one fails. Next, try a review yourself.

visual.title: Agree the handover and the way back
visual.alt: Agree one output owner and a checked way back before the handover.

check.prompt: On handover day, Growlink’s Zone 1 schedule stays active as a backup while Crop Steering runs Zone 1. Is that safe?

options.text: No; disable one so the valve has a single owner
options.feedback: Right. Two owners can double-water or leave the valve open. Keep a rollback, not a second schedule.

options.text: Yes; a backup schedule is safer
options.feedback: A live second schedule is a competing controller. The rollback plan is your backup.

options.text: Yes, if their start times differ
options.feedback: Different times still mean extra shots. One output needs one owner.

slides.title: Your turn: the name matches, the method is unknown
body: Old EC method unknown; new field wants pore-water EC
Valve name matches, but nobody traced it
Park both mappings; keep the current checked owner
slides.narration: Now review a different record yourself. Pause after each fact and decide. Fact one: the old sensor is labelled EC, and nobody knows how it was measured. The Crop Steering field expects pore-water EC, the salts in the water between substrate pieces. Fact two: the valve’s friendly name matches, but no one has traced it to the real valve. Look at the cues on screen. Both gaps stay open. A familiar-looking screen cannot close them. So park both mappings. That means leave them out for now and list them as unresolved. Investigate the EC method, and trace the valve with the installer. Meanwhile the zone stays with its current, checked owner, here Growlink. Once both gaps are closed, finish the checks from lessons C three to C five. Then plan lesson C six’s two stages. A guess here could feed the Controller a wrong number or switch the wrong valve. Next, prove the zone.

visual.title: Your turn: the name matches, the method is unknown

check.prompt: Old record: EC 3.1, method unknown. Crop Steering’s field wants pore-water EC. What do you map?

options.text: Nothing yet; leave it unmapped and find out the method
options.feedback: Right. Park the mapping and investigate. Guessed EC misleads the Controller.

options.text: The old sensor, because 3.1 looks normal
options.feedback: A normal-looking number can still be the wrong kind of EC.

options.text: The feed tank EC entity instead
options.feedback: Feed EC is not pore-water EC. Swapping it in hides the gap.

slides.title: Prove one zone before expanding
body: At handover: shutdown, owner change, then C6 stages
Check fails: new output stays off, follow the rollback
Expand one zone at a time, repeating every check
slides.narration: A builder proves one room is watertight before plastering the next. Do the same with zones. At the agreed handover, follow the approved shutdown and ownership steps. Then run lesson C six’s commissioning on this zone. Remember the two stages: an installer-run equipment test with Watering OFF, then a supervised Controller cycle. Look at the cues on screen. Check acknowledged mapping, fresh readings, measured flow and water stopping. Check approved targets and light timing too. Supervise the first enabled cycle, and record its event and the final state. If any check fails, keep the new output off and follow your rollback. Expand only when this zone’s record is complete. For example, Zone one passes on Monday. Zone two still needs its own catch, stop and supervised cycle, even if it looks identical. Keep the old records and the rollback until every zone is proven. After the quiz, lesson D one opens the Overview screen you will use every day.

visual.title: Prove one zone before expanding

check.prompt: Zone 1 passed every C6 check. Zone 2 uses the same valve model and dripper layout. What does Zone 2 need?

options.text: Its own handover, catch test, stop check and supervised cycle
options.feedback: Right. Each output is proven separately. Identical parts can be wired or plumbed differently.

options.text: Nothing; Zone 1 already proved the design
options.feedback: Zone 1’s record covers Zone 1 only. A crossed wire on Zone 2 would go unnoticed.

options.text: A catch test only
options.feedback: Catching water is one item. Mapping, stopping and the supervised cycle are needed too.

practice.prompt: Build a one-zone Growlink handover sheet: original records, physical labels, checked new entity IDs, one owner per output, crop-care cover, commissioning gates and rollback steps.
hints: Mark anything you cannot confirm as unknown, rather than guessing.
If you have no Growlink system, complete the sheet for the made-up Room A, Zone 1.
practice.success: The sheet keeps the original records, links each new entity ID to traced equipment, names one owner per output and lists checked rollback steps. Zone 1 is proven before any other zone moves.

quiz.prompt: What is the first useful step in a migration from Growlink?

options.text: Observe and record one existing zone and its owner
options.feedback: Right. Record today’s working setup before you change control.

options.text: Disable every existing schedule at once
options.feedback: That leaves plants without water and removes your baseline. Change one zone at a time.

options.text: Assume every Growlink probe connects to Home Assistant
options.feedback: Compatibility needs checking against each probe’s documents.

quiz.prompt: Old and new fields are both labelled EC. What must you check?

options.text: Measurement method, location and units
options.feedback: Right. Feed, runoff, bulk and pore-water EC are different measurements.

options.text: Only whether the numbers look similar
options.feedback: Similar numbers can come from different measurements.

options.text: Nothing; all EC fields are interchangeable
options.feedback: They are not. Feed EC is not pore-water EC, for example.

quiz.prompt: May Growlink and Crop Steering both command the same valve during migration?

options.text: No; one controller owns each physical output
options.feedback: Right. Crop Steering may observe read-only, but only one system sends commands.

options.text: Yes; their schedules sort out conflicts
options.feedback: Neither system knows the other exists. They can double-water or fight.

options.text: Yes, while the new dashboard is open
options.feedback: An open dashboard changes nothing. Ownership must be single.

quiz.prompt: One moved zone passed its supervised checks. What next?

options.text: Record its final state, then repeat every check for the next output
options.feedback: Right. Evidence for one output never commissions another.

options.text: Enable every other zone without testing
options.feedback: Untested zones can hide wrong wiring or plumbing. Prove each one.

options.text: Delete the old records and the rollback plan
options.feedback: Keep them until every zone is proven. They are your way back.

body: Overview › All zones: every zone, grouped by room.
Selected room: one room, chosen with its room chip.
slides.narration: Think of a block of flats. Flat two in one building is not flat two in the building next door. Zones work the same way. Remember from A one: a zone is a group of plants watered together. A room is a space with its own lights, and it holds one or more zones. Open the isolated demo, the practice copy that runs no equipment, and select Overview, the screen for checking rooms and zones. Its first tab, All zones, shows a card for every zone, grouped by room. The second tab, Selected room, shows one room at a time. Across the top, each room has a small button with its name, called a room chip. Select a chip, then select a zone card. That opens the zone page: one page about one zone. Zone two in Room A and Zone two in Room B are different addresses. Next, you check how fresh the information on that page is.

options.feedback: Right. The room chip sets the room; the zone number only means something inside that room.

slides.title: Check when each source last reported
body: Top bar: how long ago the Controller last reported.
Each probe keeps its own last report time.
slides.narration: Yesterday’s weather report cannot tell you if it is raining now. Every number on screen has an age too. Remember from C one: Home Assistant collects readings and switches equipment. Each named reading or control inside it is an entity, and each entity keeps the time of its own last report. Look at the top bar, the strip across the top of every page. Beside the room chips, it shows how long ago the Controller last reported for this room. That regular message from the Controller, saying it is running, is called a heartbeat. A probe has its own last report time. The Equipment screen, on its Probes tab, shows it for every probe. Here is an example. The top bar says the Controller reported one minute ago. The moisture probe last reported at nine in the morning, and it is now one in the afternoon. From nine to one is four hours, so that moisture reading is four hours old. Check each source’s own age before you trust its number. Next, read the reason the Controller gives.

check.prompt: Top bar: Controller reported 2 minutes ago. The VWC probe last reported at 06:00. It is now 11:00. How old is the VWC reading?

options.text: 2 minutes
options.feedback: That is the Controller’s heartbeat. The probe keeps its own report time: 06:00.

options.text: 5 hours
options.feedback: Right. From 06:00 to 11:00 is 5 hours. The fresh heartbeat does not refresh the probe.

options.text: It cannot be known.
options.feedback: It can. Subtract the probe’s last report time from the time now: 11 − 6 = 5 hours.

slides.title: Read the reason beside the state
body: Zone page: phase, last shot and Why / next action.
Why / next action: the reason now and what it waits for.
slides.narration: When a bus is late, the board at the stop usually says why. The zone page has the same kind of board. On the zone page, find three things. The phase, which you met in B two. The last shot. And the panel called Why slash next action. That panel gives the Controller’s reason for what it is doing now, and the condition it is waiting for next. Here is an example. The zone is in P two. The last shot was at nine twelve. The panel says it is waiting for moisture to fall to the re-water threshold of sixty percent. The probe reads sixty three percent. Sixty three minus sixty is three points still to dry, so no shot is due yet. That pause is the rule working as designed. The Controller’s records say what it decided; to see that water reached the plants, you look at the pots. Next, you put these pieces together in a worked example.

check.prompt: Zone in P2. Last shot 10:05. Why / next action: waiting for VWC to fall to 58%. Probe reads 61%. What do you conclude?

options.text: A fault: no shot has followed.
options.feedback: The panel explains the wait. 61 − 58 = 3 points still to dry before a shot is due.

options.text: Lower the re-water threshold so it waters now.
options.feedback: The rule is working. A normal wait needs no target change.

options.text: No shot is due yet; 3 points still to dry.
options.feedback: Right. 61 − 58 = 3. The Controller is waiting by its rule.

slides.title: Worked example: Training East, Zone 2
body: Training East chip pressed: Zone 2, P2, last shot 09:12.
Watering and Stop all act on the selected room only.
A shared pump stops for every room it feeds.
slides.narration: Now add the two controls in the top bar. In this fictional paper example, the Training East chip is pressed, so Training East is the selected room. Zone two is in P two. Its last shot was at nine twelve. Why slash next action says it is waiting for moisture to fall. Now look at the top bar. Watering is the room’s on and off permission for the Controller. When Watering is off, the Controller starts no shots in that room, rescue shots included. Stop all turns Watering off, then switches every pump and valve of that room off, and reads each one back. Both controls act on the selected room only, Training East. One more idea: a shared pump is one pump that feeds more than one room. If Training East shares its pump with Training West, Stop all also stops that pump, so Training West loses water too. The review box warns you about this. Read it before you confirm. Next, you meet a state the screen cannot confirm.

options.text: Only Training North is affected.
options.feedback: Its valves go off, but so does the shared pump. Training South loses water too.

options.text: North’s pumps and valves go off; South loses water from the shared pump.
options.feedback: Right. Stop all acts on the selected room, and shared equipment reaches further.

options.feedback: Stop all acts on the selected room. Only equipment that room shares reaches further.

slides.title: Your turn: finish an honest record
body: Room B, Zone 1: record pump state and report age as shown.
Unknown means the app cannot confirm the state.
Mapping: the link from a screen name to a real device.
slides.narration: A fuel gauge showing dashes instead of a number does not mean the tank is empty. It means the gauge cannot tell. The app does the same. When it cannot confirm a state, it shows the word unknown. For example, the top bar reads Watering unknown when that switch is missing or not answering in Home Assistant. Now practise in the demo. Select Room B, then Zone one. Find the pump state and its report age. Write them down exactly as displayed. If a state says unknown, write unknown. Writing off instead would claim something nobody confirmed. Then check the source, meaning the real device behind the display. The link between a name on screen and a real device is called a mapping. It is set up under Equipment, Setup. You check a mapping with the person who installed it, by reading the setup, rather than pressing buttons to see what moves. Next, find another zone on your own.

options.text: Nothing, until it shows a real value.
options.feedback: Leaving it out hides a problem. Record unknown so someone checks the source.

options.text: Pump: unknown, with its report age.
options.feedback: Right. An honest record keeps the uncertainty visible.

body: Record room, zone, phase, last shot, report ages, next action.

slides.narration: Now find a zone without the example, like finding a friend’s flat with only the address. Choose any other demo zone. Write six things: the room, the zone number, the phase, the last shot time, the report ages and the next action. Then choose where the app opens. Open Settings and help, then Settings, then Display, then Default view. The default view is the page this browser shows first when you open the app. For example, choose Selected room if you check one room every morning. This choice lives only in this browser. Another person’s phone keeps its own choice, and nothing about watering changes. A saved bookmark still opens the page it points to. Return to Overview and say the selected room’s name aloud before you read any card. That habit stops you reading one room’s numbers while thinking of another. The last slide checks what you remember.

slides.title: Recall the address and control scope
body: Top bar controls act on the selected room only.
To know water stopped, look at the outlets.
slides.narration: Close your notes and answer three questions aloud, the way a pilot repeats instructions back. First: which room do Watering and Stop all act on? The selected room, the one whose chip is pressed. Second: what does unknown tell you? That the app cannot confirm the state, so you record unknown and check the source. Third: after Stop all, how do you know the water really stopped? You look at the outlets and drippers. Off on the screen is a report from software. Remember from C one: the physical shutdown is the hand-operated way to cut water or power at the equipment itself. If water keeps flowing when it should not, use the physical shutdown first, then investigate. Tomorrow, repeat the navigation with a different demo address. Work on real equipment comes after your site’s responsible person has shown you around it. Next lesson, you change one target safely.

options.text: Trust the screen; off means stopped.
options.feedback: The dripper shows water still flowing. What you see at the outlet wins.

options.text: Press Stop all again and wait.
options.feedback: Repeating a software request delays the fix. Cut the water at the equipment first.

lessons.title: Change one target and see the curve move
lessons.summary: Change one target the safe way: read who owns it, draft, review, apply, read back, then restore.
outcomes: Read Target source and say who owns today’s targets.
Tell the saved reference, the draft and the recorded lines apart.
Draft, review and apply one allowed step on the Rescue floor, then read back and restore it.
Explain why the Rescue floor is a night alarm, not a nightly target.

slides.title: Begin by reading who owns the targets
body: Irrigation › Current day › Zone › Target source.
Armed schedule: a grow plan owns targets; edit in Calendar.
slides.narration: Before you edit a shared document, you check whether someone else is editing it. Targets work the same way. Remember from B two: a target is a comparison value the Controller’s rules use. Open Irrigation, then its first tab, Current day. Choose a zone from the Zone list. Under the tabs, read the line that starts Target source. It names who owns today’s targets. Manual room targets means you set them here. Automatic setpoints means the app can adjust some targets by itself. Setpoint is another word for target. Armed schedule means a grow plan owns them. A grow plan is a dated timetable of targets, which you build in the next lesson. When a plan owns the targets, this page shows them read only. You change them in Calendar, the planning screen. For practice, pick a demo room whose Target source is not armed schedule. Two owners writing the same target would undo each other’s work. Next, look at the chart beside the targets.

visual.title: Begin by reading who owns the targets
labels: Irrigation › Current day › Zone › Target source.

options.text: Current day: type the new value.
options.feedback: Current day is locked while a grow plan owns the targets. Use Calendar.

options.text: Calendar, because the grow plan owns the targets.
options.feedback: Right. The plan’s dated targets are changed in Calendar.

options.text: Equipment › Setup.
options.feedback: Setup holds substrate, sizing and safety limits, not daily targets.

slides.title: Tell the three lines apart
body: Saved reference: the target stored now.
Draft: your proposed change, not yet sent.
Solid dark lines: what the probes recorded.
slides.narration: A recipe card, your pencil notes on it, and the meal you actually cooked are three different things. The Current day chart shows three matching lines. Remember from B one: a dashed line is a planning reference and a solid line is measured. The saved reference shows the target values stored now. The draft shows a change you have proposed but not sent. As in B one, a draft is an unsaved proposal. Here it lives only in this browser until you apply it. The dark solid lines show what the zone’s probes recorded. Use the legend to match each name to its line. Here is an example. The saved re-water threshold sits at sixty percent. You drag the draft to sixty one. The draft line moves up one point. The saved line stays at sixty. The recorded moisture line does not move at all, because it is history. Mixing these up makes people think an edit changed the plants. Next, you learn what the setting you are about to edit actually does.

visual.title: Tell the three lines apart
labels: Saved reference: the target stored now.
Draft: your proposed change, not yet sent.
Solid dark lines: what the probes recorded.

visual.alt: Actual isolated demo screen. Read the displayed room and current sample values; separate paper examples use fictional values.

check.prompt: You drag a draft target from 55% to 57%. Which line moves?

options.text: Only the draft line.
options.feedback: Right. Saved values and recorded readings stay where they are.

options.text: The draft and the recorded moisture line.
options.feedback: Recorded readings are history. An edit cannot change them.

options.text: The saved reference line.
options.feedback: The saved line moves only after Apply and a good readback.

slides.title: Learn what the setting means
body: Rescue floor: the P3 safety level for a rescue shot.
Read the ? help, unit and allowed step; note the start value.
slides.narration: A smoke alarm is not the temperature you set the heater to. It acts only when something goes wrong. Select the question mark beside a setting. This is the field help: a short note on what the setting does, when it acts and what it changes. For this exercise, find the P three setting labelled Rescue floor. You met it in B two, where growers also call it the emergency floor. The help calls it the overnight safety level of water content. In P three, the Controller gives a rescue shot each time moisture is below it. So it is a night alarm, not a level to aim for every night. Next, read its unit and its step. The unit is percent VWC. The step is the smallest change the setting accepts. We call it the allowed step. If the allowed step is one point, thirty can become thirty one, but not thirty point four. Write down the starting value before you touch anything. You need it to put things back. Next, you make the change.

visual.title: Learn what the setting means

check.prompt: A setting’s allowed step is 0.5 points. It reads 35%. Which value can you set next?

options.feedback: 0.2 is smaller than the step. Values move in multiples of 0.5.
1.3 is not a multiple of 0.5. Try 35.5 or 36.
Right. 35 + 0.5 = 35.5, one allowed step.

slides.title: Worked example: 30 becomes a 31 draft
body: Saved 30%, step 1 point: draft 30 + 1 = 31%.
Review changes lists room, setting, 30 → 31; then Apply.
slides.narration: Think of checking your online shopping basket before you pay. In this fictional paper example, the saved Rescue floor is thirty percent and the allowed step is one point. Thirty plus one step is thirty one. Type thirty one, or drag the line. The draft line moves to thirty one while the saved line stays at thirty. Now select Review changes. A review box opens and names the room the change affects. It lists the setting with its old value and new value: thirty, then an arrow, then thirty one. Read every row against what you meant to do. The button at the bottom says Apply one change. Apply is the only step that sends the value to Home Assistant, where the Controller reads its targets. In the isolated demo, Apply changes sample data only. If a row is wrong, select Back to editing instead. Next, you check that the change was accepted.

workedExample.prompt: What changes when a saved 30% Rescue floor becomes a 31% draft?

Set the draft: 30 + 1 = 31%.
See the draft line move while the saved line stays at 30%.
Select Review changes and check room, setting, 30 → 31 before Apply.

check.prompt: Review changes shows Rescue floor 30 → 32. You meant 31. What do you do?

options.text: Apply, then fix it later.
options.feedback: Fixing later means two changes and a wrong value in between. Correct the draft first.

options.text: Back to editing, fix the draft, review again.
options.feedback: Right. The review exists to catch exactly this.

options.text: Apply; one point does not matter.
options.feedback: One point on a safety level does matter. Apply only what you meant.

slides.title: Check the receipt, then restore
body: Readback: the value Home Assistant actually accepted.
Restore 31 → 30 by the same draft, review, apply, readback.
slides.narration: After you pay, you check the receipt. After Apply, you check the readback. Readback means the app reads the value back from Home Assistant and shows what was actually accepted. While it works, the button says Applying and verifying. If Home Assistant refused a value, the box says Some changes were not applied, and gives the reason. That value stays in your draft for review. If the result is unclear, for example because the connection dropped, find out what was accepted before you try again. When the readback shows thirty one, put things back. Restoring means returning to the starting value you wrote down. Thirty one minus one step is thirty. Use the same path: draft thirty, Review changes, Apply, then read back thirty. Practising the way back matters as much as the way forward. Next, try it in a different zone.

options.feedback: Right. Read the reason before trying again.

options.text: The target is 31%; the message is cosmetic.
options.feedback: The readback is the receipt. It says 30%, so 31% was not accepted.

options.text: The target is now 0%.
options.feedback: A refusal never means zero. Read the value shown and the reason.

slides.title: Try another demo zone
body: Use that zone’s own start value and allowed step.
A zone value overrides the room value for that zone only.
slides.narration: A recipe that worked in one kitchen still needs checking in another. Choose a different zone, ideally in another demo room. Use its own starting value and its own allowed step, rather than copying thirty and thirty one. Before you edit, predict which line will move. Then make one step, review, apply, read back, restore, and read back again. One more idea matters here. The Zone list also has an option called Room lights and shared targets. A value set there applies to every zone in the room. A value set on one zone overrides the room value, for that zone only. Example: the room re-water threshold is sixty percent, and Zone three has its own value of fifty eight. Zone three uses fifty eight. Every other zone uses sixty. Check which scope you are editing before you apply. Next, recall the whole journey.

options.feedback: A zone value applies to that zone only. Zone 4 falls back to the room value.

options.text: 60%, the room value.
options.feedback: Right. With no value of its own, Zone 4 uses the room’s 60%.

options.text: No threshold at all.
options.feedback: A zone without its own value uses the room value.

slides.title: Recall the complete change journey
body: Draft → Review changes → Apply → Readback; restore the same way.
Armed schedule targets change in Calendar.
slides.narration: Teach the shopping journey to someone else without looking at the screen. The draft proposes a change in this browser. Review changes shows the room, the setting, the old value and the new value. Apply sends it to Home Assistant. Readback shows what was accepted. Restoring uses the same four steps to go back. Then name the lines. The saved reference shows the stored target. The draft shows your proposal. The dark solid lines show what the probes recorded. Finally, say who owns the targets. If Target source says armed schedule, a grow plan owns them, and you change them in Calendar. Check that the demo value is back where it started, and note both readback values in your practice record. A clean record shows the next person that nothing was left half changed. Next lesson, you build that grow plan in Calendar.

options.text: A normal moisture value to hold every night.

body: Calendar: the dated timetable of the grow plan.
Profile: a named bundle of settings each day points to.

slides.narration: A school timetable says which lesson happens on which day. The lesson notes live in a separate folder. A grow plan works the same way. A grow plan is a dated timetable of targets for each zone. In Irrigation, open the second tab, Calendar. Calendar shows that timetable. Each day in it points to a profile. A profile is a named bundle of settings, like one folder of lesson notes. Before you change anything, read two things. First, the plan’s status. Draft means you can still edit it. Armed or active means the Controller is about to use it, or is using it, so editing is locked. Second, Target source, which you read in D two. In the demo, start with a plan whose status is draft. Editing a plan the Controller is following would change a live crop’s targets. Next, look inside a profile.

slides.narration: Remember the dimmer from B three. An endpoint is the set of values at one end of the slider: vegetative at zero, generative at one hundred. A profile stores both endpoints. Under Calendar, open the section called Calendar and profiles. It has three tabs: Steering balance, Endpoint profiles and Recipes. Open Endpoint profiles. Look at the two columns, one for each endpoint. One profile can serve many days and many zones. A run of days in one zone that uses one profile is called a schedule block. For example, a profile named Bulk might serve days one to fourteen in Zone one, and days one to twenty one in Zone two. That is two blocks sharing one profile. Change the profile, and both blocks change. If one zone needs different values, duplicate the profile first, then edit the copy. A shared edit can change a zone you never meant to touch. Next, work out a blend.

slides.title: Worked example: a 2%–4% blend
body: P2 shot size endpoints 2% and 4%: 2 + 0.5 × (4 − 2) = 3%.
Zone start date = day 1 for that zone.
Days 1–7 assigned; no gaps, no overlaps.
slides.narration: Halfway between two numbers sits in the middle. Shot size is how much water each P two shot gives, as a share of the substrate volume, as in B four. In this fictional profile, the P two shot size is two percent at the vegetative endpoint. At the generative endpoint it is four percent. The difference is four minus two, which is two. Half of two is one. Add one to two, and the halfway blend is three percent, before rounding to the setting’s step. The probe may rise by a different amount. Now give it dates. Open Steering balance and set the Zone start date. That date is day one for this zone. Each zone can have its own start date. If Zone one starts on the first of March, day seven is the seventh of March. Assign the profile to days one to seven, then read the blocks either side. Every day needs exactly one block, with no gaps and no overlaps. A day with no block has no targets, and the plan holds that zone. Next, store the plan and switch it on.

slides.title: Store first, then request activation
body: Review & save: checks and stores the plan, still as a draft.
Arm plan: start at the next local lights-on (activation).
Arming never turns Watering on or starts a pump.
slides.narration: Booking a flight, checking in and boarding are separate steps. A grow plan has the same kind of steps. First, Review and save. The app checks the draft for problems, then stores it in Home Assistant. A saved plan is still a draft. Second, Arm plan. Arming is a request: start using this plan at the next local lights-on. The Arm plan button stays unavailable until the Controller reports that it supports plans. Third, activation. Activation is the moment the Controller takes over the plan’s dated targets. Example: you arm at three in the afternoon, and lights-on is at six in the morning. From three in the afternoon to six the next morning is fifteen hours, so activation comes fifteen hours later. Check the status the Controller reports, not only your click. Fourth, and separate from all of these, is the Watering switch in the top bar. Arming never turns Watering on and never starts a pump. Next, learn how to hand control back.

slides.title: Understand the return handover
body: Disarm plan: manual targets return at the next lights-on.
Edit again only when the status reads draft.
Plan hold: no plan steering, but safety watering still runs.
slides.narration: A shift handover happens at a set time, not halfway through a task. Disarm plan asks the Controller to go back to manual targets at the next lights-on. Until then, the plan’s targets stay in force. Wait for the status to read draft before you edit. From then on, the plan is yours to change again. A plan hold is a different thing. A hold happens when a zone’s day in the plan is missing, finished or invalid. The Controller then stops steering that zone by the plan, rather than invent targets. Safety watering still runs during a hold, such as the overnight rescue shot below the Rescue floor. So a hold pauses the plan, and the zone can still get water. If water flows when it should not, use the physical shutdown at the equipment first. Disarm plan and a hold are software states, and they come after that. Next, practise a second block on your own.

body: Save, arm, activation and Watering are four separate things.

slides.narration: Close the screen and teach the timetable idea to someone else. What does a profile contain? Two endpoints, one at each end of the slider. When is day one for a zone? slides.title: A budget and a statement answer different questions
body: Timeline: Controller records, newest first.
Water use: litres per zone. Compare runs: two runs side by side.
Grows: run records with names and dates.
slides.narration: A budget says what you planned to spend. A bank statement shows what was actually spent. The app has both kinds of information. Targets are the budget. History is the statement. Open History in the isolated demo. It has four main tabs. Timeline is one list of the Controller’s records, such as shots, phase changes and target changes, newest first. Water use shows the litres each zone was given today, this grow week and since the grow started. A run is one grow in one room, from start to finish. Compare runs puts the run in progress beside an earlier run, week by week. Grows holds the run records: the name, start date and end date of each run. Before you open any tab, write down your question, the room, the zone and the time period. For example: did Zone two in Room A get more water on day ten than last run? A clear question tells you which tab to open. Next, make sure two runs are fair to compare.

slides.title: Match the comparison before calculating
body: Match grow age, zone, plant count, units and EC type.
Coverage: how much of the period has records. Missing ≠ zero.
slides.narration: Comparing one child’s height at age five with another’s at age eight tells you little. You compare at the same age. Grow age is the number of days since a run started. Compare day ten with day ten. Next, match the zone. Check it had the same plant count and the same setup in both runs. Then match the units and the type of EC. Pore-water EC and feed EC are different measurements, as you learned in A five. Last, check coverage. Coverage means how much of the period actually has recorded data. In Compare runs, the section called Data quality and history coverage shows each day’s recorded range as a bar. Example: one run has twenty four hours of records for day ten, and the other has six hours. That is not a fair match. A day with no records stays empty, and empty is different from zero. Next, try a fair comparison.

body: Same zone and plant count; complete day-10 records.
A: 12 L estimated; B: 15 L estimated; 15 − 12 = 3 L.

slides.narration: Now a fair comparison. Two fictional runs have complete day ten records for the same zone, with the same plant count. Run A shows twelve litres of estimated delivery. Run B shows fifteen. Subtract twelve from fifteen. That is three. So Run B received three litres more estimated delivery on day ten. Remember from B four: delivery is water supplied through the drippers, runoff is water that drains out, and uptake is water that enters the plant. Water use counts delivery, worked out from each shot’s runtime and the configured dripper flow. Keep the word estimated in your sentence. Three litres more delivery does not show the plants took up three litres more, or that a target change caused it. Climate, plant size and other changes can all play a part. A careful sentence is: Run B shows three litres more estimated delivery on matched day ten. Next, date the reference you compare against.

slides.title: Date the reference as carefully as the reading
body: Target reference: what you compare readings against.
Snapshot: targets saved at one moment, with a time stamp.
A run recorded late gets today’s targets, not past ones.
slides.narration: A budget is only useful if you know which month it was written for. A target reference is the same. Here, a reference is the set of targets you compare the readings against. In Compare runs, open the full-resolution chart and select a Target reference. There are three choices: Current configured daily plan, Saved run daily reference, and Current phase reference. A snapshot is a copy saved at one moment, with a time stamp. When you save a run record in Grows, the app saves a snapshot of the targets at that moment. Example: today is the twentieth of October, and you record last month’s run for the first time. Its snapshot holds today’s targets, not last month’s. Targets nobody saved cannot be rebuilt. Read the note beside the reference. It says when the reference was captured and where it came from. Comparing old readings with the wrong month’s targets leads to false conclusions. Next, label the delivery figure correctly.

slides.title: Your turn: name what the estimate means
body: Runtime × configured flow = estimated delivery, not uptake.
Per plant = zone total ÷ plant count: an average.
slides.narration: A taxi meter estimates the fare from time and distance. Delivery figures work the same way. The app multiplies each shot’s runtime by the configured dripper flow. That gives estimated delivery. Measured delivery would need a water meter or a catch test. Complete the sentence in your head: runtime times flow estimates delivery, not plant what? Pause. The answer is uptake. A per-plant figure adds one more step. It divides the zone total by the plant count from setup. Example: twelve litres across six plants is twelve divided by six, which is two litres per plant on average. Some plants may have had more and some less, if a dripper was blocked. When you copy a number into a report, keep its label beside it: measured, estimated or unknown. A label lost in a report becomes a false fact for the next reader. Next, try a messy comparison.

slides.narration: Comparing one day’s shopping with a whole week’s would make the week look expensive. Here, one record covers day six only. The other covers days one to six. One run is also missing its pore-water EC readings. Are their totals comparable? Decide first. They are not, because the periods differ. Choose a matched period with good coverage, such as day six in both. Why might data be missing? Home Assistant stores past readings in a part called the Recorder. The Recorder keeps readings for a limited time, and that time is called retention. Older readings are removed. Water use can also read Home Assistant’s long-term statistics, which are kept with no time limit. A longer chart cannot bring back readings the Recorder removed. The matched period. The units. The source of each number. And the coverage. Those labels let the next person check your comparison instead of trusting it. slides.title: Repair the evidence before turning the dial
body: Make safe → preserve → investigate → verify.
Water that will not stop: physical shutdown first.
slides.narration: If a fridge thermometer’s battery dies, turning the thermostat colder does not fix the thermometer. A fault is anything that stops the system working as it should. Examples are a dead probe, a valve that will not close, or a wrong reading. A fault needs a repair, not a new target. Use the same four steps every time, in this order. One, make safe. If water keeps flowing when it should not, use the physical shutdown first. Remember from C one: the physical shutdown is the hand-operated way to cut water or power at the equipment itself. Two, preserve. Write down what you saw, with times, before anything changes. Three, investigate. Find the real cause with competent help, meaning someone trained on your site’s equipment. Four, verify. Prove the fix worked, with fresh readings and a look at the equipment. Example: a reading drops to zero at two o’clock. Changing a target would leave that reading broken. Next, work through an old reading.

slides.narration: A note on the fridge saying the milk is fine means little if it was written last week. In this fictional example, a zone is holding. Holding means the Controller is giving it no shots for now. The zone’s moisture reading was last reported at six ten. It is now ten ten. From six ten to ten ten is four hours, so the reading is four hours old. Lowering a threshold would leave the old reading in place. Instead, follow the four steps. Make safe: nothing is flowing, so the zone is already safe. Preserve: record the room, the zone, the time and the reason shown in Why slash next action. Investigate: open Equipment, Probes. Read the probe’s health, such as Silent or Not reporting. Then, with competent help, check its cable, its power and its mapping, the link between the name on screen and the real probe. Verify: wait for fresh readings and a normal status before you think about targets again. Next, two readings that disagree.

slides.title: Conflicting tank evidence needs a real check
body: Tank display 80%; low float says low: conflicting evidence.
Keep protections on; look at the tank, then check each sensor.
slides.narration: If a car’s fuel gauge shows half full but the low fuel light is on, one of them is wrong. A tank level sensor measures how full the feed tank is. Some tanks also have a low float: a floating switch that reports low when the water drops past it. Here, the tank display says eighty percent, but the low float says low. That is conflicting evidence: two sources that cannot both be right. Averaging them would invent a level, and choosing eighty because it reassures you would hide the fault. Keep the protections switched on. When a tank level is mapped, the Controller holds shots at eight percent or less, or when the low float reads low. That hold stops the pump running a dry tank. Look at the tank itself, safely. Then check each sensor’s mapping, calibration and last report time. Record which check settled the disagreement. Next, a saved setup the Controller has not accepted.

slides.title: A stored setup needs Controller acceptance
body: Saved: the new setup revision is stored.
Acknowledged: the Controller confirms the revision it accepted.
Commissioned: a supervised water test proves outlets run and stop.
slides.narration: Posting a letter, the letter arriving, and the reader acting on it are three different events. Setup changes have three similar stages. If you skipped the setup lessons, here they are in plain words. Equipment, Setup is where an administrator links each zone to its real valves and probes. That link is the mapping. Each saved version of the setup gets a number, called a revision. Stage one: Save configuration stores the new revision in Home Assistant. Stage two: acknowledgement. The Controller reports which revision it has accepted, like a signed receipt. Check that it matches, and that the heartbeat, the Controller’s regular report that it is running, is recent. Until the Controller accepts the revision, keep the room’s Watering switch off. Stage three: commissioning. Commissioning is a supervised test with real water. It proves each valve feeds the right drippers and then stops. Next, the most urgent case.

slides.title: Your turn: OFF displayed, water flowing
body: Off on screen, water flowing: physical shutdown first.
Then check for a sticking valve, siphon, wrong mapping, old timer.
slides.narration: A light switch in the off position with the bulb still glowing tells you the switch is not the whole story. The screen says off, but water is visibly flowing. Finish the first response aloud: physical shutdown. Close the water or cut the power at the equipment, using your site’s procedure. Then investigate with competent help. There are four common causes. A sticking valve is a valve that stays partly open after it is told to close. A siphon, which you met in C one, is water that keeps running downhill through the pipe on its own. A wrong mapping means the screen controls a different valve. An old timer or another system may still switch the same valve. Remember from C one: each output needs one owner. Stop all, Disarm plan and a plan hold are all software requests, so they come after the physical shutdown, not instead of it. Next, write a fault report.

slides.narration: A good doctor’s note says what happened and when, before guessing why. In this case, a shot ran for Zone two, but Zone two’s moisture did not rise. Zone three, next door, rose instead. Write the observation first: room, zone, event time, what you expected and what actually happened. Example: Room A, Zone two, shot at ten fifteen, expected a rise of about two points, saw none. Zone three rose two points at ten seventeen. Then list possible causes without choosing one. The valves may be mapped the wrong way round. The probes may be in the wrong pots. Delivery may have failed. Check the zone names, the times and the commissioning records. Arrange checks with competent help, rather than switching valves one after another to see what happens. Leave out passwords and access tokens, the digital keys that let software sign in. A clear report lets someone else find the cause quickly. Next, recall the sequence.

slides.title: Recall the repair sequence
body: Make safe → preserve → investigate → verify.
Verify: fresh readings, normal status, agreed physical state.
slides.narration: Teach the four steps to someone else without notes: make safe, preserve, investigate, verify. Then explain how repairing a sensor differs from changing a target. A repair fixes the information. A target change tells the Controller to aim somewhere else, using whatever information it has. Verifying means fresh readings and a normal status. It also means a look at the equipment in its agreed final state, such as valves closed. After a valve or mapping repair, a supervised commissioning test may be needed again. Ask your site’s responsible person what you do not yet know about the physical shutdown. Where is it? What does it switch off? Who may use it? Finish your record with the fault, the repair evidence and the name of the person doing the next check. Next lesson, you build a short daily routine.

lessons.title: A five-minute daily check and a useful handover
lessons.summary: Run a short preflight, keep a five-part diary, make one reasoned decision, treat the AI assistant as advice to check, and leave a handover the next person can use.
outcomes: Run a preflight and complete the five-part daily record.

slides.title: A short preflight, then a brief diary
body: Preflight: a quick check before you decide anything.
Five parts: identity, state, water, feed and context, decision.
slides.narration: Before take-off, a pilot walks round the plane with a checklist. That short check is called a preflight. After landing, the pilot writes a log. Use the same rhythm each day. First, a preflight: a quick look at the screens and the room before you decide anything. Then a daily diary: a short written record of what you found and what you decided. The diary has five parts. One, identity and freshness: which room and zone, and how old each reading is. Two, state: the phase and the reason. Three, water: how much was delivered. Four, feed and context: the tank, the EC and the room conditions. Five, the decision. About five minutes is a good routine on a normal day. A fault takes as long as it needs. If a source has no current reading, write unknown, as you learned in D one. Next, fill in the first four parts.

slides.title: Fill the first four parts with evidence
